26282ee96a6f94b3: RIYADH: Saudi Arabia said on Friday that three people including a pilot were killed in attacks on Riyadh's international airport the day before, after Yemen's Houthis claimed a series of attacks targeting the facility.

The conflict between the Houthis and Yemen's Saudi-backed government has spilled over into the kingdom, with the Iran-backed fighters staging repeated attacks on Saudi targets since launching a lightning offensive just across the border.

In addition to seizing large swathes of territory along the Red Sea coast in Yemen, the Houthis have used missiles and drones to attack Saudi transport hubs, oil facilities and other civilian targets in the world's largest crude exporter.
The Saudi civil aviation authority said two attacks on Thursday on the Saudi capital's airport and a Saudia airlines plane there "resulted in the martyrdom of three citizens."
The national flag carrier confirmed the death of the aircraft's captain, expressing "profound sadness."
The Riyadh attacks forced diplomats stationed there to shelter in place and international schools to take safety measures, as explosions echoed across the city on Thursday.

Numerous flights at Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport were delayed or cancelled, and the kingdom's civil defence agency said missile "interception debris" had damaged a kindergarten and a medical complex in the city.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree on Friday appeared to suggest that planes would need to seek the group's permission to fly in or out of the transit hub.
"Humanitarian flights to and from Riyadh Airport will be permitted for all flights authorised" by a Houthi coordinating body in Sanaa, he wrote on X.
- 'ADVANCES ARE LIMITED' -

Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government forces it supports have struggled to reverse the Houthis' advance, despite a counter-offensive aimed at recapturing territory including the area around the Bab al-Mandab strait, which is crucial to global shipping.
While a Saudi diplomat said on Friday that Riyadh-backed forces had successfully retaken the area, a military source on the ground gave a conflicting account, saying fighting was ongoing.

The Yemeni military source told AFP that government forces had launched a "major operation" in the strait region, supported by Saudi air power, but added that "fighting is fierce and advances are limited."
Houthi-affiliated media, meanwhile, said an attack by government forces south of the strait had been repelled.

A regional source told AFP on Friday that Riyadh would not bow to the Houthis' "military blackmail" and would not agree to a truce until the Yemeni government regained all the territory it lost in recent weeks.
The Houthis' Al-Massirah TV channel reported fresh Saudi strikes on Sanaa, shortly after a large demonstration in support of the group in the city centre.
The raids targeted military positions far from residential neighbourhoods, according to an AFP correspondent.
Houthi media had also announced strikes during the night targeting two factories in the capital, as well as in Saada governorate, the group's stronghold.

The Houthis, whose heartlands are among the Zaidi Shia Muslims in the northwest, had already controlled the capital Sanaa and most of Yemen's major population centres since the start of the war in 2014.
Riyadh's military coalition intervened to support the government the following year.
- EVACUATION WARNING -

After declaring the start of their counter-offensive against the Houthis, Yemen's government claimed to have pushed the fighters out of strategic areas on the Red Sea coast and the port city of Mocha.
But the Houthis insist they are holding their territory, and military sources from both sides contacted by AFP have not reported any major changes on the ground.
The Houthis have also warned workers to evacuate Saudi Arabia's oil facilities, having days before hit a major refinery south of the capital.
Admissions by Saudi authorities of civilian targets being hit are relatively rare. There have been few statements on Houthi attacks in recent weeks.
Claims by the warring parties have been impossible to independently verify, with the situation moving fast and access for journalists difficult.
In Yemen, one of the world's poorest countries, ordinary civilians are paying the price for the renewed fighting, with more than 200,000 people displaced since July, according to UN data.--aFP

422c70a25c1016fe: THE HAGUE: The International Criminal Court said Friday that US sanctions on the institution were an attack on international law and warned that "history will judge this moment."

The sanctions are "an assault on the rule of law and on the very foundations of the international legal order which strikes at the simple principle that no one stands above the law", said the court in a statement.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said earlier Friday that Washington would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court," escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump's administration against the court.
The court said such actions were aimed at intimidating ICC staff and disrupting its activities, vowing it would not be deterred.

"The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane in the statement.
The statement called on the ICC's 125 members to side with the institution, saying: "Its fate now rests also in the hands of the states that created it."
"Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an institution created to protect them came under attack," said the court.--AFP

02462b24d25108ee: GEORGE TOWN: The 2027 Budget is expected to strengthen Malaysia's northern corridor as a hub for high-value investments, semiconductors, artificial intelligence (AI) and advanced manufacturing.

The Northern Corridor Economic Region (NCER) welcomed the budget announcement, saying its focus on technology, innovation, talent development and industrial growth would support the region's economic development.

Northern Corridor Implementation Authority (NCIA) chief executive Datuk Mohamad Haris Kader Sultan said the Budget aligned with the NCER Strategic Development Plan 2026-2030, which prioritises high-value industries, human capital development, inclusive growth and competitiveness.
"The budget also recognises key economic projects and ecosystems across Perlis, Kedah, Penang and Perak," he said.

Haris said in Perlis, infrastructure development at the Chuping Valley Industrial Area, strengthening of the NCER Agribio Economic Zone and enhancement of Perlis Inland Port are expected to support the state's ambitions in agrotechnology and cross-border trade.
In Penang, he said a RM100 million Strategic Investment Fund to support semiconductor and advanced manufacturing companies is expected to reinforce the state's role in the technology sector.

"Kedah will continue to benefit from the development of Kulim Hi-Tech Park as a destination for global semiconductor investments, strengthening the region's high-technology ecosystem and creating skilled job opportunities.

"In Perak, the development of Lumut Maritime Industrial City and the Automotive Hi-Tech Valley in Tanjung Malim is expected to expand investment opportunities in the maritime, automotive and future mobility sectors, while supporting local vendor development," he said.

Haris also welcomed the government's announcement of RM1.2 billion in investments by Khazanah Nasional Bhd and the Retirement Fund Inc (KWAP) to strengthen local semiconductor companies, alongside the SemiconStart programme and initiatives to develop startups and AI capabilities.
He said these measures would support NCER's role in the national semiconductor industry, particularly through the Penang-Kedah ecosystem and the NCER Technology Innovation Centre.

The proposed Sovereign AI Cloud Malaysia, increased research and development funding, and plans to develop 200,000 AI workers would also create opportunities for the region to emerge as a regional digital innovation and technology hub, he added.
The budget also allocated RM8 billion for technical and vocational education and training (TVET), alongside skills training and talent development initiatives.
"These measures will help develop a skilled workforce to meet industry demand in semiconductors, AI, advanced manufacturing, smart logistics and the digital economy.

"NCIA will continue working with the federal and state governments, investors, industry players and academia to translate the budget initiatives into realised investments, quality jobs, talent development and sustainable, inclusive economic growth," he added.

He said the northern region's strengths in semiconductors, AI, cross-border logistics, automotive, maritime industries and agrotechnology positioned it to attract quality investments and create high-value employment.

In his 2027 Budget speech, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim announced that the government would provide an additional 100,000 free artificial intelligence (AI) subscriptions, expanding access to new AI applications, including ChatGPT, under the 2027 Budget.
He said the initiative would be expanded following an encouraging response to the existing free AI subscription programme for young people.
Anwar also said the government would develop a sovereign AI cloud to keep Malaysians' data and the country's strategic information under national control.
afd8fb0a0229b4d4: KUALA LUMPUR: The RM2,500 starting salary for semi-skilled workers and graduates announced in Budget 2027 should not come at the expense of existing allowances or employment terms, said the Malaysian Islamic Youth Movement (Abim).

Its president Ahmad Fahmi Mohd Samsudin said the job categories covered, employer coverage, effective date and implementation mechanism for the rate needed to be clarified to ensure workers could benefit from the initiative.

"Enforcement must ensure that the benefits of an increase in basic wages are not eroded through reductions in allowances or changes to employment terms that disadvantage workers," he said in a statement.

When tabling Budget 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat today, the Prime Minister announced that the government would introduce a minimum monthly salary of RM2,500 for graduates and semi-skilled jobs as an initial step under reforms to the workers' income framework.
Anwar said the measure aimed to ensure that wages received by workers were more commensurate with their qualifications and skills.

Commenting on the increase in the minimum wage to RM2,000, which will take effect in June 2027, Ahmad Fahmi said Abim recognised the capacity of micro, small and medium enterprises (MSME) to bear higher wage and contribution costs.

However, he said the exemption for MSMEs with annual sales below RM50 million needed to be clarified, particularly in terms of its scope, duration and the number of workers excluded from the new rate.
He said the government should provide a transition plan with clear timelines and targeted support to improve productivity based on the actual capabilities of businesses.
"The sustainability of businesses and workers' right to earn a decent wage must be safeguarded together," he said.

Meanwhile, he described the maintenance, insurance and contribution assistance package jointly funded by the government and Grab as a positive step, adding that its coverage should also be clarified and protection extended to workers across different platforms.

"The setting of minimum income rates must take into account net income after work-related costs, with the involvement of workers' representatives and effective dispute resolution channels. Social protection must remain continuous when a person uses multiple platforms or changes jobs," he said.

He said the automatic registration of citizens as members of the Employees Provident Fund at the age of 18 should be accompanied by contribution assistance for young people with low or irregular incomes.

He said opening an account must be followed by the ability to build savings, while housing and business financing should be aligned with borrowers' repayment capacity, supported by affordable rental options near workplaces, as well as mentoring and market access for young entrepreneurs.
444f2eb867ada504: WASHINGTON: The United States on Friday imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, vowing to cripple the tribunal's operations just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to a former ICC judge who warned of mounting political attacks on the court.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court," escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump's administration against the Hague-based tribunal.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said in a statement.
The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that "history will judge this moment."

The move came on the same day the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the peace prize to South Africa's Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old jurist who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal, served on the ICC and later led a UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.
Rubio's statement did not mention Pillay or the Nobel award.
Instead, he said the sanctions were needed to protect security personnel and elected officials from prosecution by a court the United States has never joined.

"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said, adding that the measures would cut off the court's resources and cripple "its ability to operate."

The top US diplomat said Washington had for more than a year spelled out "basic gestures of good faith" it expected from the court, and had held off on the designation in hopes that the ICC or its member states would change course.
He said no "meaningful steps" were taken to address US concerns.

Rubio also called on US allies that belong to the court and "rely on American service members for their defence" to rein it in, warning that otherwise Washington would keep working to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick."

The Trump administration had previously sanctioned individual ICC officials, including its prosecutor and several judges, over the court's investigations involving the United States and Israel, which is also not a member.
Trump last month called on all ICC member states to quit the body, denouncing it as "out of control" and a "rogue institution."--AFP

e059bd41592400a8: PETALING JAYA: The tax reductions for micro, small, medium enterprises (MSMEs) address rising costs, which remain a key barrier to growth, says one of the world's largest professional accounting bodies.

“Tax relief, together with expanded financing support, should improve cash flow and strengthen the ability of MSMEs to invest and expand their business,” CPA Australia’s tax committee member Tai Lai Kok said in a statement.
Earlier today, Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the government would reduce income tax rates for MSMEs by 1% next year, when tabling the 2027 budget.
Under the budget, the tax rate on the first RM150,000 of chargeable income will be reduced to 14%, while the rate for chargeable income between RM150,000 and RM600,000 will be lowered to 16%.
The tax cut was proposed in response to concerns from SME entrepreneurs facing rising operating costs, Anwar said.

Separately, the government’s decision to increase individual income tax relief and lower tax rates for selected middle-income earners could help improve disposable income at a time when many households continue to face cost-of-living pressures.

fc52a879b2af9ce6: AYER KEROH: A 2.74m-long green anaconda named Diana has given birth to 10 offspring at the Melaka Butterfly and Reptile Sanctuary after going nearly seven months without food.
The sanctuary's managing director, Gerard Wong, said Diana gave birth on Monday after a gestation period of about 190 days.
He said the birth marked a milestone in wildlife conservation, as the offspring represent the second generation of green anacondas bred at the sanctuary.
The births bring the sanctuary's green anaconda population to more than 40, making it home to Malaysia's largest population of the species.
"This is meaningful because Diana was born at the sanctuary in August 2020.
"This second generation proves conservation and breeding efforts involving exotic species native to South America can be carried out in Malaysia," he said at a press conference today.
Unlike most snakes, which lay eggs, green anacondas give birth to live young. They typically go without food throughout their gestation period, which lasts about six to seven months.
Wong said the birth demonstrated the sanctuary's expertise and facilities in breeding exotic reptiles.

He said breeding green anacondas, among the world's largest snake species, required meticulous care, particularly in maintaining suitable temperatures, water cleanliness and currents that mimic their natural habitat in the Amazon Basin.
"Besides serving as an educational attraction, Diana's breeding has given our team an opportunity to document and better understand the reproductive process of green anacondas," he said.
Wong said the sanctuary had also hatched 23 baby caimans, another reptile native to South America, including the Amazon Basin.
The sanctuary plans to organise a carnival soon to allow visitors and animal lovers to see the baby anacondas and caimans up close.
f65300bbe9300ef9: Punching the air and roaring in Unison, ecstatic crowds joined a growing demonstration on Wednesday in support of Pakistan's jailed former prime minister Imran Khan, an opposition show of force that authorities had sought to avert.

Supporters of Khan's Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party began their so-called "long march" on Sunday, demanding his release and airing anti-government sentiment fuelled by harsh economic conditions.

"I joined this procession for one reason: Imran Khan's release. I will not return under any circumstances until he is released," 58-year-old Qalandar Khan said in northwestern Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, ruled by the PTI.
"If the government and the establishment think they can remove Imran Khan... they should know that he has a place in our hearts," said the protester from the mountainous North Waziristan area.
A hugely popular former cricket star, Imran has been behind bars since August 2023 and faces scores of charges from corruption to treason following anti-establishment riots also in 2023.
He and his legal team reject the allegations, branding them as politically motivated cases aimed at neutralising his popularity.
"Imran Khan wanted to establish peace in the country and eliminate corruption," said protester Pir Fayyaz, 40, a property dealer from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.
"We have become deeply frustrated with inflation, lawlessness, poor governance and terrorism in the country," he added.
"We are Khan's soldiers," Sohail Afridi, PTI chief minister for Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, shouted down a microphone as he addressed crowds south of Peshawar city, ahead of the fourth day of the march.

From atop a truck with a five-metre-high platform festooned with smiling pictures of the jailed former prime minister, Afridi reiterated PTI demands including access in prison to Imran for doctors, party officials and relatives.
Raising his fist in the air, Afridi asked the crowd: "Are you ready to march to Islamabad?"
The packed crowd of protesters, some holding red-and-green party flags or clutching pictures of Imran, cheered back: "We are ready."

A police intelligence official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said there were 1,500 vehicles and some 5,000 to 6,000 people travelling within the convoy in the PTI's Khyber Pakhtunkhwa stronghold.

With fears of potential violence, authorities have been preparing for weeks for the possible arrival of demonstrators in the capital Islamabad, with the march originally slated for Sept 27 and then postponed until Sunday.

On Tuesday, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif urged the PTI to call off the march and re-enter negotiations with the government. Talks between the two sides hit an impasse early Sunday before the march began.
The Pakistani premier also warned of the demonstration's negative impact on the economy, saying that undermining the government's efforts would be met with the force of law.
The march is yet to pass outside the confines of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, leaving open the possibility of an agreement between the opposition and the government to end the demonstration.
"We are not taking the law into our own hands," 40-year-old Bismillah Jan said from the march.
He added, however, that: "All party workers, including myself, are ready to make any sacrifice for Imran Khan."
The demonstration pressed to Khyber tribal district, with the PTI and Pakistan flags flying, music blaring from loudspeakers, and vehicles showered in flower petals.
Farmer Changiz Khan, 58, was dressed in the red and green colours of Khan's party.
"The country is currently experiencing a continued decline," he said. "We believe that after Imran Khan's release, the country will return to the path of development.
"We will continue the struggle until we achieve our objective and gain control over our own land."

e82f1f4c592541da: KUALA LUMPUR: Mercy Malaysia is rolling out its Haze Emergency Response nationwide to supply medical aid and health guidance to vulnerable groups as air quality worsens across several states.

In a statement today, the humanitarian organisation said the initiative builds on its ongoing efforts in Sarawak, where it has supported public health advocacy, community awareness and assistance for those affected by haze.

"Haze is currently affecting several parts of Peninsular Malaysia, including Johor, Negri Sembilan, Melaka, Selangor and Kuala Lumpur. Severity varies from place to place, but the risk to vulnerable groups remains.
"Children, older persons, pregnant women and people with respiratory or heart conditions face the greatest health risks," it said.

With the Northeast Monsoon approaching, Mercy Malaysia is preparing for possible haze-related needs in western parts of the country and elsewhere by monitoring conditions, assessing emerging needs and coordinating with relevant stakeholders.

As part of its response, the organisation has prepared Haze Emergency Response Kits containing loratadine, wet wipes, normal saline, lozenges, a KF94 face mask, a small clear pouch and a health information flyer.

Mercy Malaysia urged federal and state authorities and relevant agencies to keep coordination strong, issue timely and clear public health advisories, support high-risk groups and speed up assistance to affected communities.
Mercy Malaysia president Datuk Dr Ahmad Faizal Mohd Perdaus said tackling haze required collective action involving government agencies, civil society, the private sector and the public.

"Haze is not something any one agency, community or individual can manage alone. It takes collective action as a nation," he said, urging the public to follow health advisories, protect their families, check on neighbours and support communities most affected.
He said cooperation among all parties was essential to ensure information, protection and assistance reached affected communities promptly.

Mercy Malaysia is appealing for public and corporate contributions to support the preparation and distribution of haze response kits, public health advocacy and assistance for affected communities. - BERNAMA

A resurgent Verstappen, who won for the first time this season in Malaysia last weekend, clocked 1min 31.156sec under lights at a Marina Bay Circuit enveloped in haze caused by fires in Indonesia, 0.120sec quicker than Russell.
"It's always close here in Singapore. And also your lap itself, you're pushing as hard as you think is possible, close to the walls in places," said the four-time world champion.
"Once we bolted on the soft tyres (for SQ3), it felt like the car was coming alive a little bit more, but I did not expect this.
"Of course, very happy to be first."
Fifth was the McLaren of Lando Norris, followed by the Ferrari of Lewis Hamilton.

Championship leader Kimi Antonelli, sporting a new aerodynamic package, was only seventh in his Mercedes, with Liam Lawson (RB), Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) and Pierre Gasly (Alpine) completing the top 10 on the grid.
Verstappen has never won in Singapore, where extremes of heat and humidity play a part in the most physically attritional race of the season.
He was buoyed by the pace of his Red Bull, which traditionally struggles on slower speed and bumpy street circuits.
"I think the last few races we have been a lot stronger," said Verstappen.
"But this track still highlights a few little weaknesses in the car, but we manage to drive with them as well as possible."
However the Dutchman could face a grid penalty as he was being investigated by stewards after the session for allegedly overtaking Hamilton under yellow flag conditions during SQ1.
Russell said of P2: "It is going to be challenging, the grip here (means) the drivers on the pole side have a big advantage."
- 'Difficult weekend' -
Antonelli admitted he struggled throughout the session.
"Still a lot to understand about this package, the car is very unpredictable and it is very hard to put a lap together," said the Italian, who is 84 points ahead of Russell in the drivers' standings.
"I came with high hopes. But I think it will be a difficult weekend. I don't really see where we can find seven tenths."
Singapore is featuring a sprint race for the first time, on a track that is notoriously difficult for overtaking.

The only practice session for the teams to get to grips with the idiosyncrasies of the Marina Bay Street Circuit took place on a dusty track before sunset earlier on Friday, hardly ideal preparation for a 62-lap night race on Sunday.

Singapore is exteremly tough on drivers, who can shed up to 3kg (6lb) during the grand prix from sweating alone, and the race weekend has been declared a "heat hazard" by organisers allowing drivers to wear cooling vests.

The teams also have to contend with the thick haze caused by wildfires in nearby Indonesia, which saw Singapore's air quality plunge to an "unhealthy" 205 on Friday according to the IQAir tracking website.
Readings above 150 are classified as unhealthy, while levels above 300 are considered hazardous.
Motorsport's governing body told AFP the race was not under threat from the haze.

be9296b3befb9853: BENGALURU: EV-maker Tesla has started calling its "Full Self-Driving" feature "Tesla Assisted Driving" on its European websites, dropping a name regulators have said was misleading, as CEO Elon Musk pushes for EU-wide approval for the software.
The rebrand comes after Germany said on Tuesday Tesla had offered to switch to the new name. Musk has described the self-driving technology as key to the company's future growth.

Tesla's FSD page for Slovakia now redirects to a "Tesla Assisted Driving" page, as do pages in other European countries such as Germany, Spain and the Netherlands. The US site still refers to it as "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)."

A Reuters report published this week detailed how Tesla mounted a campaign to win approval for FSD in Europe, including encouraging owners and supporters to lobby national regulators for faster approvals.

In September, a Norwegian Tesla owner asked the Norwegian Public Roads Administration whether Tesla's changes to how it described FSD addressed concerns about the name, according to documents Reuters obtained through freedom-of-information requests.
"Please do not simply say again that 'we are waiting for the EU' without explaining what Tesla or Norway must deliver in the meantime," the owner said.
Several regulators have said the old name is misleading because the system requires constant supervision and drivers remain legally responsible.

In Sweden, consumer protection authorities had earlier asked the Swedish Transport Agency to assess whether the marketing of FSD could give buyers the false impression the system was capable of fully autonomous driving.

In Italy, authorities had said in internal government correspondence that the name "Full Self-Driving", together with Tesla's promotional material, "could lead users to believe that the vehicle is equipped with unsupervised automatic driving functions attributable to higher levels of automation, particularly SAE Level 3", in communication seen by Reuters through freedom-of-information requests.
Eight EU countries already allow the system, with Slovakia expecting to become the ninth within days.
An EU-wide vote has been pushed from October to at least December, with countries like France conducting additional testing.

34199cd5b889185a: Sarawak bade farewell to a towering political legend in the person of Datuk Song Swee Guan this week. He died of old age at 84 after a short hospital stay.
Song had served four terms as a state assemblyman representing Padungan in Kuching, now an opposition stronghold. In addition, he was Bandar Kuching member of parliament from 1995 to 2003.
A stalwart of the Sarawak United People's Party (SUPP), a component of the state ruling coalition, Song was probably best known for being the first mayor of Kuching South.
Through much of the 1980s, he had served as chairman of the then Kuching Municipal Council (KMC). When Kuching was elevated to city status in 1988, Song became its founding mayor.
He retired from politics after serving a term as speaker of the Sarawak Legislative Assembly.

A life-long bachelor and son of a long-serving KMC chairman, Song Thian Cheok, Song's political star was somewhat dimmed in later years when rather serious personal financial misfortune required the intervention of party leaders.
Sarawak Premier Tan Sri Abang Johari Openg has described Song as a humble and dedicated public servant.

"The late Tun Taib (Sarawak's chief minister who went on to become Yang Di-pertua Negeri) even recommended him (Song) to contest in Padungan and Bandar Kuching. And he won. That shows how strong his grassroots support was," Abang Johari noted.

Current Sarawak Legislative Assembly Speaker Tan Sri Mohamad Asfia Awang Nassar, who had served as deputy to Song, noted that in Song, SUPP had a popular political figure who contested in Bandar Kuching against another political legend, the late Sim Kwang Yang of DAP.
"We had a strong DAP man and Song managed to defeat him. As such, he was the only one who became mayor, MP and state assembly speaker.
"He was also considered a popular hero," Asfia reminisced.

In that sense, Song represented a revival of political fortune for SUPP which had suffered setbacks after it became part of the state government in 1970, culminating in the defeat of then deputy chief minister Tan Sri Stephen Yong in a Kuching constituency in 1974.
After Song's triumph in Bandar Kuching, no other SUPP candidate has been able to wrest back Bandar Kuching from the DAP.

In Kuching, the Chinese-majority SUPP seems to face a classic Chinese-voter dilemma: how to be a consequential party in government while maintaining Chinese voters' desire for real political checks and balance.
The state assembly now has all of only two opposition members from DAP, who won at the expense of SUPP.
SUPP must hope that the revival it experienced after the late Tan Sri Adenan Satem became chief minister would undergo a further boost in the coming state election.
That revival was reinforced after Abang Johari took over from Adenan and won the last state election by a landslide.
The nostalgia kindled by all the public tributes generated following Song's demise may serve to further entrench SUPP's political comeback.
The writer views developments in the nation, region and the wider world from his vantage point in Kuching

6ee1d780ca9711ca: With schools in half of the country ordered closed in view of the worsening haze, the command by the king to prioritise the health of schoolchildren is well taken.
The sudden school closures as pollution readings inch towards highly "unhealthy" levels are more than just a health emergency.

It has also disrupted the lives of parents who must find guardians for their children while they are at work. It is natural for Malaysians to blame Indonesia, where the forest fires—often deliberately set—originate.
More so when this has been a recurring problem during the dry season for more than two decades.

We wonder how many more school closures, disrupted flights, hospital admissions and weeks of inhaling unhealthy air will it take before the haze is treated as a standing regional emergency rather than a seasonal inconvenience.
Malaysia has rightly sought Indonesia's cooperation. Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim has spoken to Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto, who assured him that necessary steps are being taken.
Malaysia's offer to assist in putting out the fires has been accepted by Indonesia but protocols must be streamlined so precious time is not wasted before joint action begins.
Public fury in Malaysia over the haze is understandable but must be tempered with empathy for Indonesians in southern Sumatra and Kalimantan, who are suffering from even worse chocking conditions.
If anything, the fury of Indonesians over their authorities' lacklustre response to the fires and culprits must be growing.
Our hope is that Indonesians themselves will demand an end to this haze pollution once and for all. Assurances from the top Indonesian leadership, however welcome, cannot be the endpoint.
The recurring nature of transboundary haze demands concrete action, accountability and prevention, rather than crisis management every time the skies turn grey due to man-made causes.

That said, instead of turning public fury over the haze into a diplomatic confrontation with Indonesia, it is far more fruitful to welcome Prabowo's commitment to get to the root of the problem and work together for mutually beneficial end results.
However, Malaysia must make clear that good neighbourliness does not mean accepting the same crisis year after year.
Indonesia needs to demonstrate that its assurances translate into real, long-lasting effective action on the ground.
Malaysia and Asean as a whole, meanwhile, need to work to strengthen the mechanisms to prevent another haze episode ever becoming a region-wide public health crisis again.
School closures should serve as a wake-up call. Children should not have to stay home because governments fail to prevent a problem that has been recurring for decades.
1915e47be7373e03: Large-scale AI training has already escaped the confines of a single datacenter. Google said Gemini was trained synchronously across clusters in multiple locations; Microsoft has connected AI data centres in Wisconsin and Georgia into what it describes as one distributed AI supercomputer; AWS has connected AI compute clusters across wide areas to allow Anthropic to build Claude models; Meta has built high-capacity datacenter interconnects to support model training; and CoreWeave and Google Cloud recently announced cross-cloud training with a private interconnect, with Azure likely to follow later in the year. This growing geographic spread of model training is partly due to the limits of single datacenters or campus clusters, which can be strained as they try to meet the compute and power demands of new models. Cisco estimates that training models today can require clusters with tens of thousands of GPUs. By 2030, the largest individual frontier training runs could draw 4-16GW of power, according to researchers at Epoch AI. Distributing compute allows hyperscalers and datacenter operators to build in locations with more available power or space and fewer planning constraints. How to train an LLM At the core of an LLM is a neural network with billions of numerical parameters, or weights, that are adjusted during training. A batch of training data passes through the model, which makes a prediction. The system measures the error and calculates how the weights should change. The weights are updated and the process starts again. At the scale of modern models, this work is distributed across thousands of GPUs and other accelerators, such as AWS Trainium and Google TPUs. Different GPUs can process separate batches of data or different parts of the model. But they cannot work entirely independently: at various points they must exchange results and synchronize before the next stage of training can begin. What networks carry between the accelerators is generally not the text or images used to train the model, but large arrays of numerical data such as gradients and intermediate results. Thousands of accelerators may need to exchange and combine that data at roughly the same time. "If you look at any training job, it is basically a repetition of compute and synchronization," explains Ramesh Sivakolundu of Cisco's Silicon One architecture team. "You compute the weights, communicate those weights to synchronize every GPU in the cluster, and then restart the computation. That means bursty traffic happens periodically throughout the training process." Thousands of accelerators can finish a computation phase and start communicating at the same time. This can lead to "incast" problems where many senders converge on the same destination and traffic arrives faster than the next link can handle. The fundamental issue lies with synchronization. In a synchronous training job, one group of GPUs cannot simply ignore a slower group and continue independently. The network-wide exchange must complete before the participating GPUs can move on to the next stage. A network delay therefore becomes compute delay. "You don't want the network to be the bottleneck in the training process," says Sivakolundu. "The idea is to keep the GPUs fully occupied and not have the network introduce additional latency into the overall training program." That does not mean that every instance of network congestion or packet loss brings the entire model training to a complete halt. However, a delayed or dropped flow may require retransmission, prolong a collective communication operation, and leave other accelerators waiting. More serious failures can require training to return to a saved checkpoint. Different kind of interconnect "Inside a single datacenter, you can assume you have built a full network connecting the GPU racks with the bandwidth you planned for," says Itamar Gold, director of product management at Cisco. Gold’s point is that with scale-across, coordinated AI workloads may have to traverse a more constrained inter-site fabric than the network within each facility. Instead, he says, traffic destined for the other facility may be funneled through what is effectively a narrower pipe. A synchronized burst can turn that pipe into a temporary choke point. Traditional DCI connects otherwise independent datacenter environments, and is typically built for redundancy, reach and workload distribution. The traffic that runs over them is often replication traffic or application data, and the flows are asynchronous, meaning one flow does not have to finish in lockstep with the others. In scale-across AI training, the inter-site network becomes part of a coordinated distributed computation rather than simply moving data between otherwise independent systems. It is therefore essential to have sufficient bandwidth and predictable delivery. From rack to region Within a rack, bandwidth requirements can be enormous – up to 800Gbps-1.6Tbps - but the distances are short. High-speed serial lanes combine to make a GPU cluster appear as a single compute unit. When the AI fabric is extended across an entire facility, “scale out”, racks will still require connections up to-1.6T. At these data rates, copper is generally confined to short reaches. Connections across rack rows and datacenter floors instead use pluggable optics, with scale-out links extending from hundreds of meters to around 2km. “Scale-across” extends a coordinated AI fabric across multiple facilities, making inter-site network behavior part of workload performance. Depending on the architecture, those links may span metro or regional distances, and potentially farther depending on the architecture. According to Cisco modelling of large distributed AI deployments, aggregate bandwidth requirements can reach roughly 14x a conventional DCI baseline. For starters, short-range datacenter optics are not designed to carry 400-800 Gbps signals over hundreds of kilometers. For these distances, operators need coherent optics that use sophisticated modulation and high-performance digital signal processing to keep high-rate optical signals usable over metro and regional fiber spans, compensating for physical impairments that become more pronounced with distance. The number of ports matters too. Cisco estimates that connecting two 100MW AI sites could require 12,000 to 32,000 coherent optical ports at the scale-across layer, compared with roughly 1,000 to 2,000 for conventional DCI between comparable facilities. At 400G or 800G per port, that adds up to multi-petabit aggregate capacity. Moving that much data is also a power and space problem. Coherent pluggables put the coherent transponder function directly into router or switch ports, avoiding a separate bank of standalone DWDM transponders. Cisco says this reduces the additional rack space, power and cooling needed for the inter-site optical layer which is an important consideration when the AI factories themselves are already power-constrained. The latency problem Even with sufficient bandwidth and suitable optics, distance adds latency. If congestion develops, the network needs time to signal the sender to slow down. Over a local AI fabric, feedback can arrive quickly. However, if the connection is stretched across 100 km of fiber, considerably more data can be transmitted before the sender even learns that there is a problem. Cisco calculates that on an 800 Gbps connection spanning 100 km, around 100 MB of data can already be in transit during that feedback interval. Cisco argues that these longer feedback loops increase the value of networking silicon designed with substantially deeper buffering. The shallow-buffer switching architectures designed for very low latency inside a datacenter have less capacity to absorb traffic while congestion feedback crosses a long-distance link. "The reason you need deeper buffers as the distances get longer is that you don't get feedback about the transfer of packets for a longer period of time," says Sivakolundu. "If you don't buffer deeply enough, you can end up dropping and retransmitting packets, increasing latency." Deep buffering absorbs a temporary burst or disruption while traffic management and congestion signaling address the underlying problem. Sustained congestion still needs more capacity or a change in how traffic is distributed. The same buffer also helps with oversubscription. If the combined capacity feeding into an inter-site connection is greater than the capacity of the link itself, a synchronized burst can arrive faster than the link can drain it. Buffering gives that excess traffic somewhere to wait without getting dropped while congestion controls respond. Rather than dividing the available buffer into fixed amounts for each port, a shared buffer is a common pool of packet memory that can be allocated wherever congestion appears. That lets a busy link absorb a larger burst without dropping packets. "The longer you're reaching out, the more you may need to buffer," says Gold. "You also need the flexibility to put as much buffer as possible where it is needed, perhaps on one port or a few ports where you've identified a problematic flow. Our approach is a single, fully shared buffer." AI training does offer one useful characteristic: much of its collective communication is repetitive and therefore more predictable than DCI traffic. Cisco's approach is to use proactive congestion management to steer or schedule traffic before a predictable burst creates a problem, while retaining deep buffering as a safety net for transient congestion and unpredictable events such as a link failure. The two approaches are complementary: one tries to avoid the queue while the other gives the network somewhere to put the traffic when a queue forms. Cisco’s bet on co-design Cisco’s scale-across architecture uses the Silicon One P200, a 51.2 Tbps programmable, deep-buffer routing processor included in the Cisco 8223 and Cisco N9000 platforms. Those systems can be paired with Cisco's 400G and 800G coherent pluggable optics for the long-distance links, while open line systems such as Cisco Open Transport 3000 and Cisco NCS 1014 handle the optical transport layer where required. Coherent pluggables generate the DWDM wavelengths directly from the routing system, while the line system amplifies and carries those wavelengths across the fiber plant. For links requiring multiple parallel fiber pairs, Cisco's Open Transport 3000 uses a multi-rail design that combines the optical components for multiple rails onto one line card. Cisco claims this reduces power per rail by 75 percent and rack space by 80 percent. Where a separate transport system is required, the NCS 1014 can provide 12.8 Tbps of capacity from a 1RU line card. The P200 has a programmable run-to-completion network processor and P4 tooling, which Cisco says allows protocol support, telemetry and other packet-processing features to be developed in software rather than making every change dependent on a new silicon generation. For scale-across, where operators are still testing different topologies and traffic-management methods, "the same programmable flexibility can let network functions evolve without every new requirement forcing a chip replacement,” says Sivakolundu. Cisco also includes hardware-based protection for inter-site traffic in that design, its argument being that encryption should not create another processing bottleneck for the training fabric. A key part of Cisco's pitch is the co-design. A networking ASIC is defined years before the finished router reaches a datacenter. Cisco argues that because its silicon, system and optics teams sit within the same company, requirements for port density, buffering, power, telemetry and the optical interfaces can feed back into the chip design rather than the system team receiving a commercial ASIC and working out what it can build around it. That does not mean scale-across has settled on a single approved architecture. Cisco itself divides the problem into campus, metro, and regional deployments, and different operators are experimenting with various combinations of networking and training techniques. Implementations vary significantly by operator, including distance, topology and workload design, while the common problem is maintaining coordinated AI performance across sites. The technology is still at an early stage, however. "We are seeing early deployments now, but it is a process and I think it will take a few years," says Gold. Designing a network for distributed training will not eliminate the latency of distance, but it can keep that interconnect from becoming the bottleneck. That gives hyperscalers and datacenter operators the flexibility to add compute where power and space are available, while still treating multiple sites as part of the same training infrastructure. 1aa1345afc978f48: WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The ICC's deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal's work.

The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges. Friday's move would go far further, by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement.
"That is why, today, the US is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate."
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Khan told Reuters the sanctions "must be condemned".

"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan said. "Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."

Washington has long been angry over ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan which the ICC has since closed.

The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the Nato alliance apart from the US and Turkey.
It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and Nato member.

Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work in international criminal justice, served as a judge on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003-2008. In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack".
"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world," the committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.

He did not provide further details, but a senior State Department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licenses "to protect American interests", an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions.
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organization, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.

The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during his first term, which were rescinded under President Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.

Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.

The court's registrar Osvaldo Zavala Giler called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called "blocking mechanism" that lets it shield European countries from the extra-territorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the US had delayed its sanctions hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.

"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said.

"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said.

6fad125a5c83f089: OSLO: The Nobel Peace Prize was awarded Friday to South Africa's Navi Pillay, the judge who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal and presided over a UN commission which accused Israel of genocide in Gaza – a move angrily denounced by Israel.
The 85-year-old, who is currently a judge on the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in a case in which Myanmar also stands accused of genocide, has spent her career defending international law.
She dedicated her award to the "survivors of international crimes", speaking Friday from the courtroom in Nuremberg, Germany where the trials prosecuting World War II Nazi leaders took place.
Pillay has been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted," said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, the chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee in Oslo.
Israel's foreign ministry said the award legitimised "anti-Israel hatred", and that Nazi propagandist Joseph Goebbels must be "applauding from hell."

The daughter of a bus driver in a family of Tamil descent, Pillay's career has taken her from South African courts, where she defended anti-apartheid activists, to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court (ICC).
She headed the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry (COI), which does not speak on behalf of the world body, and which last year found that genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Pillay told AFP at the time that her team had shared "thousands of pieces of information" with prosecutors at the International Criminal Court.
Israel had categorically rejected the report's findings, slamming it as "distorted and false."
Pillay's "independence, her expertise and steadfastness have made her one of the most respected international jurists of our time," the Nobel committee said.
In Nuremberg, Pillay said world leaders have a "legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war", and criticised attacks on the ICC.
"We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack," she said.
"This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court," she continued.
US President Donald Trump last month called for all ICC member states to quit the body, denouncing it as a "rogue institution."
Earlier, she reacted to the news about her prize by making a quip about Trump's well-documented desire to win the prize himself.

"If you clap a little bit more I may share this prize with Trump," Pillay said earlier during a standing ovation captured on video by Amnesty International Secretary General Agnes Callamard in Nuremberg and posted on the social network X.
- 'COURAGE TO SPEAK THE TRUTH' -
The Nobel committee said that while its prize honoured Pillay's career of fighting genocide, it was not taking a stand on whether Israel's actions in Gaza constitute a genocide.
Pillay noted that many had paid tribute to her courage in that report.
"You can imagine how surprised I was. Why would you need courage to speak the truth?"

The UN said her prize was a "testament to the need and to the value of human rights in this world more than ever", while the ICC said her award was of "particular significance" given the attacks on international law.
The prize for Pillay is sure to anger Trump, whose administration has repeatedly attacked international justice institutions.

"This is a clear message to those who are putting pressure on these institutions, to those who are sanctioning the judges and are attacking the institutions. That needs to stop," Frydnes told AFP after the announcement.

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, Trump has made no secret of his desire to win the prize, insisting that he was the most deserving candidate and claiming to have ended up to eight wars.

But his war against Iran, his territorial expansion ambitions as in Greenland, his hard line on migrants, and his attacks on multilateralism and the media have, according to experts in Oslo, disqualified him for the prize.
The prize comes with a gold medal, a diploma and a prize sum of US$1.2 million.
The award will be presented at a formal ceremony in Oslo on December 10, the anniversary of the 1896 death of the prize's creator, Swedish inventor and philanthropist Alfred Nobel.--AFP

81599d1b93a82c55: PETALING JAYA: Persekutuan Pekilang Malaysia (FMM) menyuarakan kekecewaan terhadap Belanjawan 2027, menyatakan terdapat kekurangan dari segi sokongan kepada sektor perkilangan.

2334718bbfb8caeb: PETALING JAYA: The Malaysian Pharmacists Society (MPS) has called on the government to clarify the status of contract pharmacists and provide a clear pathway for those awaiting permanent appointment.

ba43c6afd53b5665: MANILA: Prosecutors said Friday they are dropping a bribery charge against Philippine Vice President Sara Duterte, who still faces three other charges at her ongoing impeachment trial that could lead to her removal from office.
The 48-year-old is also charged with misuse of state funds, unexplained wealth, and an alleged assassination threat against one-time ally President Ferdinand Marcos.
If the Senate finds her guilty on any of the charges, she will be stripped of the vice presidency and permanently barred from elected office, ending her bid to become president in 2028.
Prosecutors from the House of Representatives, which voted to impeach Duterte in May, said the decision to drop the bribery charge would speed up the trial, which hit its 37th day Friday.

"We think we have presented enough (evidence). To drag it further might be stretching the patience not only of the people but also the senator-judges," Congressman and prosecutor Jonathan Keith Flores told reporters.
Prosecutors have already presented evidence and witnesses in support of the assassination and misuse of funds charges.
On Friday, prosecutor Jose Manuel Diokno told the court they had presented their last witness in the hidden wealth case. That witness will be cross-examined on Monday.
The Senate had originally given prosecutors 60 trial days to present their case, after which Duterte will present her own witnesses and evidence.
Last month, in a ruling widely seen as a blow to Duterte, the 24-seat Senate approved a lower threshold of votes needed to find her guilty, potentially making it easier to execute her ouster.

With at least four senators loyal to the vice president now absent from the trial – two in jail, another in hiding and a fourth on extended medical furlough abroad – only 14 votes are needed to find her guilty.
Senators voted that the constitutionally required two-thirds guilty verdict by "all members of the Senate" referred only to those "capable of participating."--AFP

0ad68807f4c6de80: KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia ended a nine-year wait to return to the Suhandinata Cup final after producing a superb 2-0 win over arch-rivals Indonesia in the semi-finals of the World Junior Mixed Team Championships in Cairo on Friday.
The national juniors prevailed 55-49, 55-42 in another fiercely-contested Malaysia-Indonesia battle under the 55-point relay format to reach their first final since 2017.
Malaysia had to do it the hard way in the opening game after Tiew Wei Jie went down 6-11 to Fardhan Rainanda Joe in the opening boys' singles segment.

Genevie Lim-Low Zi Yu responded strongly to swing Malaysia ahead 22-17 in the girls' doubles, only for Indonesia to regain the advantage at 33-32 after Carine Tee's girls' singles clash with Jolin Angelia.

The pendulum swung again when Ahmad Redzuan-Low Zi Yu edged Malaysia 44-43 ahead through the mixed doubles before Damien Ling-Irfan M Shazmir delivered under pressure in the final boys' doubles segment to seal the game 55-49.
Malaysia carried that momentum into the second game.
This time Wei Jie gave them an 11-7 start before Genevie-Low Zi Yu stretched the advantage to 22-11.
Indonesia refused to go away, cutting the deficit to 33-28 after the girls' singles, but Ahmad Redzuan-Zi Yu restored Malaysia's cushion at 44-37.
Isyraf Hafizin-Ahmad Redzuan then showed no nerves in the decisive boys' doubles segment, closing out the contest 55-42 to spark Malaysian celebrations.

The victory was especially significant against an Indonesian side who have been among the Suhandinata Cup's most consistent performers in recent years, winning the title in 2019 and 2024 and finishing runners-up last year.
Malaysia's only triumph in the world junior mixed team event came in 2011, while their previous final appearance was in 2017 when they finished runners-up to China.

Friday's result also continued Malaysia's recent edge over Indonesia at junior level, having beaten their neighbours 2-1 in the group stage of the Asian Junior Championships in Japan in June under the same relay format.
Malaysia will face either China or Thailand in the final.
1a03f75dc80f5d24: Oracle's new Fusion Claw runtime could give customers more control over AI agents automating business processes, analysts say. But they warn that adoption remains at an early stage and customers risk becoming more tightly tied to Oracle's applications and cloud. Having promised "applications that can reason, decide, and act in pursuit of defined business objectives" back in March, Big Red has now introduced a runtime to govern their actions, running on its cloud and integrated with its Fusion applications. Oracle is targeting ERP, finance, and supply chain management with Fusion Claw for cloud-based Fusion applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI). It will be powered by frontier models including those from Google and OpenAI, with support for others planned over time. Oracle CEO Mike Sicilia said the company was trying to address the problem of getting "measurable value for our business" from AI investment. "Fusion Claw helps answer that question by moving from AI assistance to execution, enabling customers to automate increasingly complex work across their most important business processes, with enterprise-grade governance," he said. Analysts welcomed the move as a path that offers customers control and assurance in their AI agent implementations on Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications. A recent Gartner "first take" on Fusion Claw said the technology was a way to provision "isolated containers to execute heavy supply chain optimizations and subledger reconciliations within clear policy limits" rather than running local desktop scripts or chatbot prompts. "Instead of bolting AI onto legacy transactional back ends as a sidecar copilot or UI wrapper, Oracle is rebuilding its application foundation around native agentic workflows," Gartner said. Other vendors should take heed of the move, the analyst said, because customers need to get away from prompt-based UIs and sidecar chatbots that only address routine data entry and basic task automation and offer "diminishing returns" that fail to justify enterprise AI spending. "AI horsepower should be pointed at the most complex operational challenges that were previously unsolvable inside core ERP systems, such as multi-echelon supply chain visibility, network design, sales and operations planning (S&OP), logistics routing, and load optimization," Gartner said. However, users trying to get these kinds of enterprise-scale applications hit a cost barrier because using an LLM to address thousands or millions of "transactional records, line items, or constraint variables… quickly becomes financially unviable at enterprise scale," it said. Oracle gets around the problem by separating reasoning from compute execution. An agent evaluates context, assembles tools, and defines execution logic just once, the analyst said. Calculations and multivariable optimizations are delegated to deterministic compute engines, "avoiding passing millions of records through expensive LLM context windows." Isolated containers also offer specific authority limits, business object states, and policy guidelines. After execution, the system leaves hints to skip redundant paths and cut token consumption, Gartner said. Oracle is offering ready-made applications, including ones to improve readiness of financial ledgers, make staffing plans and consolidate shipping. Gartner recommends including Fusion Claw in requests for proposals (RFPs) for AI agent deployments, although Patrick Connaughton, chief of research, enterprise applications, warned that Fusion Claw was "very much in early piloting mode still." Fellow analyst company Forrester also welcomed Oracle's introduction of Fusion Claw, which is offered under per-user or per-employee pricing as well as consumption-based models. Principal analyst Craig Le Clair said: "Commercials are in line with the aggressive positioning from the tech industry. In our view, we have many trust issues to solve before agentic systems can be trusted to create tools and process patterns independently of designer's intent." However, in contrast with Fusion Claw's Oracle-only view of the world, enterprises have hybrid environments with AI agents built within cloud domains such as Salesforce and Oracle, process platforms like Pega or UiPath and frameworks like LangChain. "Cloud domains like Oracle are best suited for more generic, non-differentiating functions that the cloud domain knows well, while more complex and transformative custom agents should look toward custom agentic frameworks and the hyperscaler platforms," he said. Lock-in is an issue. While inspired by OpenClaw, Oracle's version is proprietary and tightly coupled to the Fusion platform, Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure. "Enterprise architects are the key to avoid 'lock-in' with guidance on when to select a domain cloud over a more open platform above, pointing to data residency and external integration needs, for example. If the domain strength is strong enough, lock-in may be OK," he said. Organizations already heavily invested in Oracle may welcome tighter governance and potentially lower running costs. Those using a broader mix of suppliers may find the ties to Fusion and OCI harder to justify. ®
9367e5275cafb5ca: PETALING JAYA: Corporate figures Nazir Hussin Akhtar Hussin and Mubarak Hussin Akhtar Hussin have voluntarily taken garden leave from their executive roles at Avangaad Bhd, effective yesterday.

12df1f0e1a911aab: PETALING JAYA: The government's proposed AI-powered scam-checking app must be fast, free, simple, and continuously updated with real-time reports if it is to be of benefit to the elderly and less tech-savvy, says a crime prevention specialist.
Shamir Rajadurai of Prevent Crime Now said most victims fall for scams not because they are gullible, but because they lack a quick way to verify suspicious messages or requests.
“Scammers rely on speed and pressure. They win when victims have no time to think. Anything that puts a pause between a victim and a transaction takes away the scammer's biggest weapon,” he said.

"An AI tool that checks a number, account or link against reported cases and known patterns gives people a second opinion in seconds at the exact moment of decision. It also levels the field for the elderly and those less digitally savvy," he told FMT.

However, such a tool would be only as good as its data and usability. He said the tool must be fast, free, simple, and continuously updated with real-time reports as scammers constantly evolve their tactics.

The government's proposed app was announced in the 2027 budget tabled today. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said the National Scam Response Centre will develop the app which would allow the public to check suspicious phone numbers, bank accounts and links before making any transactions.

Shamir said the app represents a positive shift to preventing crimes before they occur. He suggested that banks follow through by integrating verification alerts directly into their apps so warnings appear at the point of payment.
Shamir said the government should also publish case outcomes and success rates to build public trust in the AI safeguard.

"Most important is investing in the officers behind the systems, because the best technology is only as effective as the officer using it. An AI alert or a flagged network means little if the officer on the ground cannot read the signals, build the case or support the victim," he said.
16a816b284a5fdc5: PETALING JAYA: The RM400 million for Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) would be used to create 120 new green spaces, conserve existing parks, upgrade public facilities and preserve the city's heritage.

f94896713563456a: LONDON: Manchester United manager Michael Carrick said he has been "personally" affected by Manchester City being found guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.
City are appealing against last week's verdicts they broke financial regulations over a nine-season period between 2009 and 2018.
Carrick was a member of the United team that finished runners-up to City in the Premier League in 2011/12 and 2017/18, prompting him to hint he feels aggrieved by the scandal.
In 2012, Sergio Aguero's last-gasp winner for City against Queens Park Rangers on the final day of the season denied United the title and launched their rivals' era of sustained success.
"I've got my own questions about it. It's affected me personally in different ways over a period of time," Carrick told reporters on Friday.

"It's unprecedented, you know, a unique situation to be in this, at this level with such a huge impact in so many ways. So, we all need to know what's going to happen, really. I think that's pretty clear."

The former England midfielder wants a swift resolution to the City appeal, with the sanctions if they fail to overturn the decision potentially including a severe points deduction, expulsion from the Premier League or even being stripped of their previous titles.
"As the case is going now, I don't know where that stands and how it's going to end up. So we'll just have to wait and see," Carrick said.
"What I will say, the sooner it gets sorted, I think for everyone's benefit, is essential."
Carrick would benefit if United were awarded any titles taken from City after their second-place finishes.
But the 45-year-old does not believe a belated medal would carry the same significance so long after the drama of each title race has faded.
"I think when you're in sport, certainly in football, the strive to win and the emotion, the feeling about winning is a lot of it is in the moment," he said.
"Once that's done, there's no getting that back in any direction. That's the feeling we all crave is coming out on top.

"It's the moment that you strive for to win and achieve in that moment, so the medal here or there, not getting blasé about it, but that doesn't bring the feeling of when you initially win or you don't win. That's essentially what we're all in it for."
Carrick needs a win to stop the focus turning to his own future after United's poor start to the season.
They are languishing in 12th place with one win from five games ahead of Saturday's clash with bottom-of-the-table Tottenham.
"Just another game. Points-wise, I think Tottenham have played a lot better than it shows at times," said Carrick, also a former Spurs player.

9573b017c0cb1ddb: BANGKOK: Thailand's Queen Suthida has flown a Gripen fighter jet solo for the first time, the royal household revealed Friday, watched on by her husband King Maha Vajiralongkorn, himself a keen pilot.
The 48-year-old queen took off in a single-seat JAS 39C from a military air base in southern Surat Thani province on Thursday, according to footage released by the royal household.
The outing followed weeks of simulator training at the base and about 10 hours in a two-seat Gripen, media reports said.
A former Thai Airways flight attendant who married the king in 2019, days before his coronation, Suthida began flying in 2010 and has logged nearly 1,190 hours.
She regularly flies as co-pilot to the king on royal trips, including landing at Bhutan's notoriously difficult Paro airport, the reports said.

Thailand already operates a squadron of Gripen C/D fighters made by Sweden's Saab, and last year signed a deal for three Gripen E jets and one Gripen F worth around US$556 million, with deliveries due by 2030.
After she landed, the king handed the queen a bouquet and pinned a Golden Gripen Order patch on her left arm, which reports said made her Thailand's first female Gripen pilot.--AFp
b6a67633c9311870: PUTRAJAYA: Chief Secretary to the Government Tan Sri Shamsul Azri Abu Bakar is confident civil servants are ready to ensure government policies, including 2027 Budget, are implemented swiftly and effectively.
He said the commitment of all civil servants was crucial to ensuring that the people could share the benefits of economic growth.

"For all civil servants, I am confident that we are always ready to shoulder these trusts and responsibilities as a National Covenant and continue to support government policies through swift and effective implementation, to ensure that the extraordinary benefits of economic growth can be felt by all," he said in a statement today.
Shamsul Azri also expressed his appreciation to Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim, who is also Finance Minister, for tabling Budget 2027 in the Dewan Rakyat today.

Themed "Reaching for the Skies, While Anchored on Our Values", the budget allocates RM459.8 billion, comprising RM376.8 billion for operating expenditure and RM83 billion for development expenditure, based on eight key priorities.
The measures announced included raising the minimum wage to RM2,000, various tax incentives and exemptions, as well as subsidies, assistance and incentives totalling RM80 billion.
The budget also provides for Special Financial Assistance of RM1,500 for civil servants and RM750 for government retirees.
