Ada banyak contoh mengenai R pertama, iaitu agama; mungkin yang paling terkini adalah satu ucapan oleh Noorazli Said, ketua Umno sebuah bahagian, yang didakwa mempersendakan paderi dan biarawati Katolik dengan 'jenaka' berunsur seksual semasa Perhimpunan Agung Umno (PAU) 2026 baru-baru ini.

Ekoran dari ucapan menjijikkan itu, pelbagai pihak termasuk pemimpin Sabah, Persatuan Gereja Sarawak (ACS), dan Wanita PKR mengecam 'jenaka' tersebut sebagai tidak menghormati agama. Malangnya 'jenaka' itu tidak berseni dan tidak boleh pula dihujahkan sebagai suatu satira. Meskipun Noorazli memohon maaf secara terbuka atas kecalaran hati dan ketergurisan jiwa serta salah faham yang timbul; 'jenaka' atau ucapan beliau itu telah merebak dan dikongsi secara meluas lantas menyakitkan hati penganut Kristian Katolik.

Manakala untuk R kedua, iaitu kaum, serba sedikit ia masih berkait dengan identiti agama. Ini kerana di Malaysia, kategorisasi agama selalu dihubungkan dengan bangsa tertentu. Pada tahun 2024 misalnya, dalam satu kes yang turut berkait dengan agama, Ahli-ahli Parlimen berbangsa India menggesa Kementerian Dalam Negeri mengambil tindakan tegas kepada penceramah berbangsa India yang telah memeluk Islam, Muhammad Zamri Vinoth Kalimuthu dan pihak-pihak lain yang didakwa menghina agama Hindu. Mereka juga mendakwa tindakan terhadap 3R yang melibatkan kaum bukan Melayu dan agama bukan Islam selalunya agak perlahan ditangani.
R, ketiga adalah institusi diraja yang mana khusus untuk mereka yang melakukan penghinaan terhadap Yang di-Pertuan Agong dan raja-raja Melayu.

Sebagai misalan, dalam satu perkembangan berkait isu yang melibatkan kedudukan Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan, Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir; tokoh politik dari Wawasan dan bekas menteri besar Negeri Sembilan, Rais Yatim didakwa mengikut Seksyen 4(1)(b) Akta Hasutan yang boleh dihukum di bawah Subseksyen 4(1) akta sama. Sabit kesalahan membawa hukuman denda tidak melebihi RM5,000 atau penjara tidak lebih tiga tahun atau kedua-duanya.

Seperti disebut awal, terdapat tanggapan pendakwaan melibatkan isu 3R kadang-kala agak berat sebelah. Meskipun dakwaan 3R boleh menimpa sesiapa pun, tidak dapat dinafikan golongan kanan dan konservatif Melayu sering menggunakan naratif 3R sebagai instrumen untuk mengukuhkan jati diri, mempertahankan status quo, dan menuntut hak-hak yang mereka percaya, sedang 'diancam' atau 'terancam'. Seringnya hujah mereka adalah 3R teras kelangsungan hidup bangsa Melayu.

Dalam hal institusi diraja, golongan kanan Melayu misalnya berpegang yang institusi diraja bukan sekadar simbol perlembagaan, tetapi penjaga dan pelindung langsung kepada hak orang Melayu dan kesucian agama Islam. 3R akan dihujahkan untuk melabel golongan progresif atau bukan Melayu sebagai 'kurang ajar' atau 'derhaka' sekiranya mereka mempersoalkan sebarang titah atau peranan institusi diraja. Ini bererti golongan konservatif boleh secara taktikal berselindung di sebalik hujah institusi diraja untuk beroleh legitimasi moral yang konon perjuangan mereka itu direstui oleh 'payung negara'.

Oleh sebab isu 3R adalah ayam gepuk atau ayam geprek untuk masyarakat Melayu yang kian konservatif, parti politik tertentu akan tanpa segan silu menunggang naratif 3R untuk memperlihatkan diri mereka sebagai pejuang hak konservatif.

Namun demikian, dalam hal di Negeri Sembilan, tindakan terhadap penentang-penentang Tuanku Muhriz dapat dikatakan sangat perlahan. Seingat saya sudah dua kali Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) menggunakan istilah penderhaka buat kelompok 'dago dagi' (derhaka dalam Adat Perpatih) dan terbaru pada 4 Oktober 2026, Dewan ini "memohon supaya pihak-pihak penguatkuasa terutamanya polis dan Jabatan Peguam Negara mengambil langkah-langkah yang sewajarnya untuk menyiasat dan memulakan pendakwaan atas kesalahan-kesalahan jenayah yang telah mereka lakukan melalui tindakan-tindakan seperti yang telah dinyatakan di atas". Menurut Dewan, "ini penting supaya mereka tidak secara terus mengambil tindakan-tindakan dan membuat kenyataan-kenyataan yang bertentangan dengan perlembagaan dan undang-undang yang akan mengelirukan pentadbiran negeri dan rakyat jelata".

Meskipun seruan DKU ini ternyata keras dan tegas iaitu agar tindakan segera diambil terhadap kelompok yang mempertikaikan keabsahan Tuanku Muhriz, pihak berkuasa ternyata sangat berhati-hati. Ramai yang percaya, tindakan penuh waspada pihak berkuasa ini kerana sistem diraja di Negeri Sembilan agak unik dan berbeza dari negeri lain.

Sungguhpun begitu, saya mempunyai pandangan berbeza. Memang mulanya perbahasan mengenai kedudukan Yamtuan Besar dan Undang itu terhad kepada pertikaian tafsiran adat. Akan tetapi sejak akhir-akhir ini sembang isu adat dikuasai oleh lasykar siber, dan lasykar siber ada tuannya. Selalunya tuan lasykar siber adalah jembalang tertentu yang berhalimunan.

Jika di alam nyata, ramai individu tidak akan berani mengeluarkan kenyataan berbaur perkauman atau menghina institusi diraja lantaran risiko sosial dan undang-undang yang jelas. Namun demikian di dalam talian, pengguna Threads misalnya boleh menyembunyikan identiti sebenar mereka di sebalik nama samaran atau profil palsu. Ada banyak akaun meragukan tanpa identiti sempurna. Mereka adalah cybertrooper berbayar. Oleh sebab mereka tidak perlu punya nama sebenar, ia memberikan rasa selamat untuk mereka bertindak agresif, memaki hamun, serta menyebarkan kebencian terhadap Yamtuan Besar tanpa memikirkan akibatnya. Hujung-hujung mereka keseronokan mendapat bayaran lebat.

Kelengahan dan kelenguhan pihak berkuasa bertindak sehingga memaksa institusi diraja Negeri Sembilan mengeluh lebih dari sekali mengenai penderhaka-penderhaka ini sebetulnya agak mencengangkan. Ia seolah-olah mereka yang melakukannya memiliki perlindungan, dan berasa kebal. Seolah-olah ada 'jembalang besar' yang merestui perbuatan mereka.

Lebih memburukkan keadaan adalah ruang digital juga mengalami budaya kongsi dahulu atau gejala 'information velocity' di mana pengguna berkongsi maklumat serta-merta tanpa perlu sebarang pengesahan. Dalam tindakan refleks, jari kita akan mudah untuk 'repost', 'retweet' atau menekan butang 'like' dan emoji. Hantaran teks, video potongan pendek, atau tangkapan layar yang dimanipulasi sering disebarkan dalam kumpulan WhatsApp keluarga atau kerjiranan tanpa perlu menyemak kesahihan. Semua ini berpotensi pula mengakibatkan ahli kumpulan bertingkah, membusut menjadi telingkah dan lama-kelamaan membukit menjadi gaduh dan kelahi.

Perlu diingat pendekatan lasykar siber dalam apa jua keadaan adalah mencipta persepsi dengan naratif sebelah pihak. Ini kerana lasykar ini adalah 'askar upahan' para politikus di medan siber. Mereka berperanan untuk mencipta atau menonokkan pandangan awam. Dengan memomokkan fakta palsu mengenai Yamtuan Besar Negeri Sembilan seperti Tuanku Muhriz kononnya cenderung kepada DAP, atau menggadai tanah adat; mereka yang melakukan hantaran begini berharap dapat mencederakan imej seorang raja yang kelihatannya begitu bersabar mendepani perangai dan tingkah laku pengkritik.

Sebenarnya Tuanku Muhriz tidak akan kudung atau puntung meski diserang bertalu-talu oleh lasykar siber. Tembaklah banyak mana pun. Memang Tuanku Muhriz tidak akan membalas pencaci hidup-hidup. Memang lasykar siber pula tidak pun sedikit rasa bersalah membuatkan Tuanku Aishah Rohani Tengku Besar Mahmud menitiskan air mata sebak dan terharu di KLIA sepulangnya dari bercuti.

Namun, sebagai pengkaji orang Melayu dari Institut Alam dan Tamadun Melayu, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, saya ingin membawa perhatian bahawa dalam kepercayaan orang Melayu; status seorang raja yang sah jurai keturunannya tidak akan terjejas. Mereka yang dakwa-dakwi raja itu yang selalunya akan terpelanting, dan hancur binasa.

Sebetulnya seruan DKU agar penderhakaan dibendung amatlah penting untuk segera ditunaikan. Gejala '3R' di Negeri Sembilan ini akan mewabak. Sudah ada beberapa akaun media sosial yang hidup kemudian tiba-tiba mati; atau mendadak timbul, kemudian gesit tenggelam; khusus dalam mempertikaikan sistem pemilihan atau penggiliran sultan atau raja di negeri lain.
Waktu itu kelak, gejala ini akan lebih sukar ditangani.
Artikel ini adalah pandangan penulis dan tidak semestinya mewakili FMT.

18f242eb550b4662: From Moaz Nair

Following his messy departure from PKR, Rafizi Ramli’s desperate, persistent snipes at the prime minister and his administration have been met with total silence—a calculated snub by political insiders to starve him of relevance.
Rafizi’s political career suffered a disastrous blow after his decisive defeat in the PKR deputy president election, forcing his humiliating resignation as economy minister.
Since being cast out, he has tried to reinvent himself as a fiery outsider, launching bitter critiques against the Madani administration from the political wilderness.

However, this sudden adversarial posture reeks of political opportunism. As the chief architect of the government's initial economic strategy, Rafizi championed, designed, and defended the exact frameworks he now desperately tears down.

Now, having fully severed ties with PKR, Rafizi and his remnants have migrated to a fragile new vehicle, Bersama, hoping to play spoiler in upcoming elections. Yet, this attempt to play the populist saviour ignores a damning reality: his political capital is almost broke, and public backlash has permanently shattered his reformist brand.
The groundswell of voter resentment

The fatal flaw of the Rafizi brand has always been the sheer impracticality of his hyped economic "formulas", which completely collapsed under the weight of executive governance. For a Malaysian electorate struggling under structural inflation, Rafizi transitioned from a once-celebrated champion of the working class into the ultimate symbol of elite tone-deafness.

Nowhere was this public backlash more toxic than during his disastrous rollout of the diesel subsidy rationalisation. His defensive, arrogant communication style during the crisis did not just alienate voters; it actively enraged them. While local traders, logistics operators, and ordinary citizens drowned in soaring costs, Rafizi chose to lecture the public from an intellectual high horse rather than offer executable safety nets.

This severe groundswell of voter resentment effectively handed his rivals an open goal, devastating the government's standing and resulting in a self-inflicted electoral bloodbath at the Sungai Bakap by-election.
This deep public cynicism was further cemented by the catastrophic pushback against the central database hub (Padu).
Envisioned by Rafizi as a ground-breaking matrix for targeted aid, Padu instead became a monument to structural incompetence and a lightning rod for national outrage.

The public responded to his signature project with widespread suspicion and dismal registration rates, while state governments—most notably Sarawak—outright rejected the database over glaring security and privacy flaws. Instead of a welfare triumph, the public viewed Padu as an authoritarian, half-baked surveillance tool that prioritised fiscal austerity over public readiness.
A spent force in political wilderness

Time and again, Rafizi’s academic models broke under pressure, wasting massive amounts of public funds and administrative hours on macroeconomic frameworks that failed to generate a single ringgit of measurable prosperity. On fuel subsidies, his stubborn insistence on replacing blanket pump discounts with a convoluted direct cash transfer mechanism faced severe pushback from logistics and financial experts, only to be ultimately scrapped for market-stable alternatives.

Furthermore, his ministerial stint exposed profound structural and interpersonal limitations. Under his watch, the economy ministry functioned like an isolated, toothless think-tank, completely lacking the fiscal muscle of the finance ministry to execute real structural shifts.

Worse, his public friction with Cabinet colleagues and party leaders eroded whatever internal leverage he had left, proving that his reputation as an erratic, unyielding rogue rendered him an operational liability.

While Rafizi may retain a legacy as a historical whistle-blower, governance requires the tedious work of nation-building, not merely reckless disruption. True leadership demands scalable, executable policy—not just bitter rhetorical tantrums from the political margins.

As Rafizi attempts to salvage his future through Bersama, trying to peel away reformist voters with a rigid doctrine of "four no's”—including a refusal to align with established political blocs—his path to an unconventional comeback appears increasingly narrow.
Political analysts point out that his new vehicle is almost certainly doomed to replicate the electoral irrelevance of past vanity parties.
For a Malaysian electorate thoroughly exhausted by economic volatility and unfulfilled promises, the currency of Rafizi’s hollow formulas has officially depreciated.
Moaz Nair is an FMT reader.

a4e6fe13e65a3232: Consumption is no longer just about what we buy. It has found its way into how we measure success.
In our pursuit of more, even the things that once existed simply for pleasure are increasingly expected to produce something in return.
I was sitting near my record player the other day, listening to Janis Joplin sing “Mercedes Benz”, a satire about consumerism and our desire for the good life.
Listening to it now, I wondered if we ever really got the joke, when I was reminded of an old belief of mine.
Books taught me words. They taught me articulation and expression. But songs taught me everything else.
Love, loss, longing, rebellion, disappointment, growing older. Long before I had the language to explain any of it, somebody had already put it into a song.

We still want the car. The house. The title. The salary. The right school for our children. I like nice things too. But somewhere along the way, the things we owned stopped being just things. They became evidence that we were doing well in life.
Then a conversation about reading made me wonder if consumption had moved beyond the things we buy.

A leader I work with had spoken at a conference about the power of reading and the written word. He later shared with a small group of us how the conversation inevitably found its way back to corporate leadership, an idea he gently challenged.
Of course it did.
Even the simple pleasures of reading must now have an outcome to measure.
A book should make us better leaders, sharper thinkers, more employable people. We exercise for performance and network with purpose. Hobbies become side hustles. Even rest needs to be productive.
When did everything, even books, have to earn its keep?
Economics studies what we consume. Psychology helps explain why we want it. Identity is where it gets personal, because what we consume can become part of how we measure ourselves.

We have always compared ourselves with others. We Malaysians are especially good at peering over the fence at relatives with supposedly greener pastures, colleagues and next door neighbours. Now, through social media, we carry millions of other lives around in our phones.
Someone earns more. Someone bought the Mercedes. Someone’s child got straight As. Someone landed a new job or promotion and announced it before breakfast.
The comparisons never end.
Malaysia has its own version of this question. We measure progress through growth, investment, income, infrastructure and development. We should. But what is enough for a country?
Shouldn’t progress also be felt around the dinner table at home?

A decent home. Good schools. Meaningful work. Healthcare we can afford. Time with people we love. Enough money left at the end of the month to breathe, and a retirement fund that makes growing old feel less daunting.

And a book read for no reason other than wanting to know what happens next, such as Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland by Lewis Carroll, where a hookah-smoking Caterpillar asks Alice the rather pivotal question, “Who are YOU?”
Maybe a good life does not need to produce something every minute. Some things should be allowed to exist simply because they make being alive a lot richer.
I looked back at the record spinning beside me.
Janis was still waiting for her Mercedes-Benz.
I think I’ll keep the records. And that wonderfully strange little book about Alice.

a843173a5365ccbb: For a while, those hoping to avoid the difficulty and expense of dealing with Adobe's Creative Suite have been able to use several free and/or open source alternatives that replicate some or all of those capabilities. Artcraft got its start last year as a "controllable AI for artists" that allows for precise post-generation editing of AI-crafted images and videos. 4d5e1f5c1fab6083: Artificial intelligence has become part of the zeitgeist. And while it’s a polarizing topic, Linda Rabieh has a unique take on AI: “It’s good for business. Our business, of humanistic thinking.” As senior lecturer in the Concourse program, one of MIT’s first-year learning communities, Rabieh has been introducing students to the “business” since 2010.  “What AI has been useful for is making very vivid to students today the question of what it means to be human,” she adds. “They’re meeting this question with a new urgency. What is intelligence? Is it only mathematical intelligence? Is it only an aggregation of information? Or is human intelligence something different?” AI is just one of countless thorny topics that bubble up in Concourse, which offers first-year MIT students a foundation in the humanities, alongside math and science General Institute Requirement courses taught by Concourse faculty. Studying “great books” and literary luminaries — Plato, Homer, Aristotle, Wordsworth and Coleridge, to name a few — provides a springboard for rich conversations and spirited debates. A “mini-liberal arts college within MIT” Concourse was founded in 1970 to enable humanities, engineering, and science faculty to collaborate on curriculum, cultivating a “concourse” of ideas. Now it’s a place, Rabieh says, “where students who come primarily to MIT for world-class science, math, and engineering can also have a traditional liberal education, exploring fundamental questions of human existence, reading the great books, engaging in intense, vigorous debate about these questions.” “I often describe Concourse as a mini-liberal arts college within MIT,” says Assistant Director Sasha Rickard ’19, an alumna of the program. “A lot of students tell us that Concourse is a big part of the reason they decided on MIT instead of [other schools].” Concourse accepts 50 first-year students each year. Johnnie Jones VI, a senior in mathematics and Concourse teaching assistant (TA) and debate fellow, marvels at the diversity of students the program attracts — “athletes, people who are interested in humanities, people who have no experience in humanities,” he says. “Somehow, 50 people every year self-select into this space, and magic happens.” Connection and “cross-pollination” Part of that magic is the sense of community that Concourse fosters. The program has a dedicated space in Building 16 with a classroom, seminar room, lounge, and kitchen. Students receive advising and participate in community events throughout the year. Since they overlap in their humanities, math, and science classes, as well as outside the classroom, they get to know each other and their instructors well. “There’s a lot of cross-pollination of conversation and ideas,” Rabieh says.  During the weekly Friday advising seminar, students gather over lunch to discuss assigned texts or hold debates. In the fall, topics focus broadly on the human condition, and in the spring, students consider practical political or moral issues such as gene therapy, immigration, and gun control. Several debates are held in conjunction with the MIT Civil Discourse Project, which has collaborated with Concourse since 2023. Many students stay involved in the program after their first year. Some serve as TAs, debate fellows, or associate advisors.  “There’s very much a sense of wanting to be guides and supports and set an example for the incoming students,” Rickard says. Upper-level students also take Concourse electives, hang out in the lounge, and participate in community events. Learning to think things through Taking multiple classes together, sharing meals, and spending time together outside the classroom — these common experiences build a level of trust that allows students to hold deep conversations. The result is a transformative experience. Rickard has noticed that incoming first-years tend to fall into two categories: those who think they already know the answers to political or philosophical questions, and those who have no opinion because they think there’s no definitive answer. Over time, she explains, “some students come to understand that they need to learn from others, and others learn that they really can think for themselves, and they do have something to say.” “Students learn the importance of judgment in non-quantitative areas,” Rabieh says. MIT students excel at quantitative reasoning, she adds, but “you can’t just show which political policy is right and which is wrong … and one reason I think MIT students shy away from those kinds of issues is because they don’t see a way to think through them. Concourse teaches them a way to think about moral and political questions in a rigorous way that isn’t quantitative.” That rings true for Jones. “Overwhelmingly, the greatest skill Concourse has given me, more than just teaching me things, is teaching me how to work through ideas myself — really making possible the ability to, even after a long day of work, sit down with a great book and have a conversation with someone who was alive 300 years ago about things that matter to me,” he says. Stewarding the “ethos of Concourse” into its next chapter As Concourse continues into its next half-century, a new leader has taken the helm. Ford Professor of Political Science Lily Tsai was recently named director after Anne McCants, the Ann F. Friedlaender Professor of History, stepped down. Colleagues laud McCants for 14 years of steady leadership; cultivating a robust, collaborative advising program; advocating for a whole-student approach; and for her passion for teaching. McCants says she relished interacting with Concourse students in a sustained way — often for all four years — and learning not only from them, but also colleagues. “Having a group of committed educators from different disciplines in sustained conversation is a remarkable feature of Concourse. In our normal faculty roles, we are siloed off from those whose fields of study are not ours. I will miss those interactions as much as I do the ones with the students.” Tsai assumes the role as the Institute expands efforts to broaden connections between the School of Humanities, Arts, and Social Sciences (SHASS) and other fields. Those efforts include the Compass Initiative, which Tsai co-leads with other faculty from across SHASS; the MIT Human Insight Collaborative; and the creation of shared faculty positions within the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. “The ethos of Concourse is thrilling to me,” Tsai says. “Through reflection and debate about what we value individually and collectively, Concourse students cultivate the skills and habits of mind that prepare them to be not only excellent engineers and scientists, but also responsible citizens and leaders. At a time when the whole world is seeking to ground our use of powerful technologies in thoughtful, principled judgment, Concourse seems all the more vital, and I’m eager to champion the teaching and learning that the program does so well.”
fc6778094f3899ce: Pennsylvania's explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it's the largest on record since 1991.

Pennsylvania's health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April, when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.

Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths—a newborn, a 6-week-old, an 18-year-old, a 20-year-old, and a 40-year-old. All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.

1c9558d381626972: Every piece of AI content from Google's Gemini models has a hidden SynthID label, which makes it very difficult to pass the content off as authentic. SynthID has also gotten buy-in from other major AI players, but actually checking for those invisible watermarks has been a convoluted process. It's going to be a little easier going forward, though. Google has announced that its SynthID detector now supports watermarks from all its partners, and it's available for anyone to use on a new dedicated website.

SynthID is an invisible signal encoded in the pixels of AI-generated images and videos, and in the waveform of AI audio. Google says Gemini alone has integrated SynthID with over 180 billion images and videos, plus 240,000 years of audio. Until now, the only way for those outside of Google's trusted tester program to check for SynthID was to ask Gemini. This is rather clunky, and the model's output could sometimes be confusing when you just wanted a simple "yes" or "no."

Now you can cut Gemini out of the loop. Starting today, you can go to the new SynthID.com website to check a piece of content for an AI watermark. A major limitation of Google's previous detector was that it only checked for Google's version of SynthID. Even though ChatGPT images, for example, have SynthID, they wouldn't be flagged in Google's detector. That's no longer a problem.
0a185023e5a9d7aa: From Ng Sze Fung
Every year, Malaysia’s healthcare debate returns to the same question: how much more should the government spend? The 2027 budget will be no different.
There will be calls for more doctors, more nurses, better hospitals, newer equipment and higher allocations.
All of these are necessary and known. But throwing more money into the same administrative structure will only get us so far.
The harder question is more structural in nature.

Malaysia runs a highly centralised public healthcare system. That model has important strengths. National financing and common standards help prevent access to healthcare from depending entirely on where someone lives.

But centralisation also creates rigidity. The healthcare needs of Selangor, Penang, Kelantan, Sabah and Sarawak are not identical, yet staffing, service planning and resource decisions still operate largely through the same federal machinery.

The answer is not simply to create 13 separate health systems. Nor can healthcare simply be “handed over” to the states. The Federal Constitution is clear. Under the Ninth Schedule, medicine and health fall under the Federal List, while public health, sanitation and disease prevention sit partly within the Concurrent List.
Any serious proposal for decentralisation must therefore work within this constitutional structure, not pretend it does not exist.

Fortunately, decentralisation need not be equated with constitutional disruption. The federal government can continue to finance healthcare, set national standards, regulate professions and medicines, and redistribute resources between richer and poorer states.
At the same time, states or regional health authorities could be given greater discretion over how services are delivered locally.

That could mean more flexibility in workforce deployment, clinic and hospital planning, maintenance spending, primary care integration and partnerships with private providers where public capacity is stretched.
Local authorities could also play a larger role in preventive health, particularly where healthcare overlaps with sanitation, urban design and community wellbeing.

The guiding principle should be simple: centralise what protects equity, decentralise what benefits from local knowledge. The biggest risk is postcode healthcare, where richer states pull ahead while poorer states struggle.
That is why financing should remain largely federal, with allocations based on population need, age, disease burden, geography and deprivation.

Sarawak could provide a useful starting point. The state has already pushed for greater healthcare autonomy under the Malaysia Agreement 1963, including greater control over healthcare planning and the decentralisation of certain regulatory functions to the Sarawak health department, arguments shaped in part by the realities of delivering healthcare across a vast and dispersed population.
Rather than treating Sarawak as an exception, its experience could serve as a practical test of how greater local discretion can operate within a federally financed health system.
Malaysia needs to make its healthcare system less administratively rigid.

If the 2027 budget is serious about reform, the debate should not stop at how much more healthcare receives. It should also ask who is best placed to decide how that money is used, and perhaps the states are the best place to start that discussion in the spirit of decentralisation.
Ng Sze Fung is a senior analyst with Bait Al Amanah, a think tank.

ce54eafcfc8a3510: The problem with the Sports Development (Amendment) Bill 2026 is not simply how much power it gives the youth and sports minister.
It is where that power stops.
The Dewan Rakyat passed the Bill on Tuesday after 31 MPs debated it, amid concerns that the proposed Section 41A could give the minister sweeping authority over sports bodies.

Under the provision, the minister may declare a sports body unlawful if it is used for purposes harmful to national security, public order or morality. The order would cancel its registration after consultation with the sports commissioner.

Minister Dr Taufiq Johari has stressed that this is not a blank cheque. He said disagreement with the government, internal disputes or unhappiness with a sports body’s leadership would not, by themselves, justify action.
He also said the provision would rely on existing laws and offences and remain open to judicial review.
Those safeguards matter but they do not remove the central question.
If the sports commissioner is supposed to be the regulator, why is the most drastic regulatory power being placed in the hands of the politician who appoints the regulator?
That is the issue Parliament should continue examining before the Bill becomes law.
A stronger commissioner, but a stronger minister too
The Bill does not merely increase ministerial power. It also strengthens the sports commissioner.

Registered sports bodies will need the commissioner’s approval before changing their name, address or constitution, while the commissioner can direct amendments to bring a constitution into line with the law. The Bill also creates a stronger enforcement and investigation framework.
That creates an awkward structure. The commissioner becomes a stronger regulator while the minister retains the power to take the most serious action against a sports body.
There are therefore two centres of authority without a clearly independent layer between them.
That raises a basic question: who regulates Malaysian sport — the political ministry or an independent sporting regulator?
The answer should not depend on the personality of whoever happens to hold the minister’s post.

The sports commissioner is appointed by the minister, while the office already has substantial regulatory powers under the Sports Development Act 1997, including registration and deregistration functions.
The new Bill adds to those responsibilities rather than creating a fundamentally separate regulator.

If Malaysia genuinely wants a strong sports commissioner, perhaps the next step should be to make the office more institutionally independent from the minister, not merely more powerful under the minister.
That could mean clearer safeguards around appointments, tenure, removal and appeals. The precise model is open to debate.
The principle is harder to dispute: strong institutions also need strong boundaries between them.

The government has said it wants better governance and accountability in sport. The test is whether the new structure makes those institutions stronger, rather than simply making the executive stronger.
Deregistration is not a minor penalty
Section 41A deserves particular scrutiny because deregistration can go far beyond stopping an association from operating.

Under the Bill, assets of a deregistered sports body can vest in the director-general of insolvency for the winding-up of its affairs and settlement of debts. A new body may seek to take over its assets and liabilities with High Court approval.
Deregistration is therefore not simply a warning or suspension. It can end a sports body’s legal existence, trigger the winding-up of its affairs and disrupt control of its assets and liabilities.
Such a power may be necessary in extreme cases. A sports body used to finance terrorism, organise violence or facilitate serious criminal activity cannot expect registration to provide protection.
The minister has cited terrorism, subversive or espionage activity, riots and violence, and serious forms of sexual exploitation and trafficking as examples of the intended threshold.
But Parliament should still ask whether those limits belong clearly enough in the law itself.

The word “morality”, in particular, can carry a wide meaning. What evidence must be produced? Who decides when the threshold has been crossed? Must the conduct involve an offence under existing law? Does the sports body get a meaningful opportunity to answer the allegations before its registration disappears?
Those questions are not obstacles to enforcement. They are safeguards against arbitrary enforcement.
If the government’s position is that Section 41A will apply only in serious circumstances already covered by law, spelling that out more tightly would strengthen the provision.
The football citizenship scandal inevitably surfaced during the debate, with MPs warning against concentrating too much authority in one political office.
But this should not become a FAM story. The more useful question is: what lessons from FAM should be written into the institutional architecture of Malaysian sport?
If the episode exposed weaknesses in governance, accountability, documentation or decision-making, the answer cannot simply be to give the government more power over sports bodies.
It should be to make the system harder to circumvent, with clearer duties, better records, transparent procedures and credible independent review.
Malaysia already has rules, registration requirements and enforcement powers. Yet 4,687 sports associations and clubs were recorded as inactive or problematic between 2020 and 2025.
The figure included 23 national bodies, 206 state bodies, 486 district bodies and 3,972 clubs, with some found to have breached their constitutions or the Sports Development Act.
The issue, then, is not simply whether the law has enough teeth. It is whether the system can make sports bodies comply and govern themselves properly.
The commissioner already has considerable authority. The bigger challenge is making the regulatory system work consistently and effectively.
That is why strengthening the office should mean more than adding powers. It should mean bolstering its independence and accountability too.

The government has also stressed the need for better governance and accountability in sport. The new legislation therefore needs to draw a clear line between legitimate public regulation and political control of sport.
The Bill has passed the Dewan Rakyat, but it is not yet law. It still has to go through the Dewan Negara before royal assent and gazettal. That leaves room to tighten the framework.
The question is not whether the state should act against a sports body that genuinely threatens national security or public order. It should.
The question is who decides when that threshold has been crossed, on what evidence, under what process and with what independent scrutiny.
The amendment strengthens both ends of the regulatory chain. The minister gets a formidable new power. The sports commissioner gets stronger regulatory powers.
What it does not yet appear to provide is a sufficiently independent middle or appellate layer.
The problem is not power. It is where the power stops.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
4f8b260b4ed41c37: Ahad lalu sebelum bermulanya Grand Prix Bahrain di Sepang, pengulas Sky Sports Martin Brundle bertanya PMX kemungkinan Malaysia menganjurkan semula perlumbaan F1 pada masa depan. Umum tahu kali terakhir perlumbaan itu dianjurkan Malaysia di litar Sepang ialah pada 2017. Nine long years ago.
"Itu harapan saya. Kami sedang berbincang," jawab Anwar Ibrahim. Meskipun jawapan perdana menteri ringkas, ia menggembirakan ramai yang berharap F1 akan kembali ke Sepang.

'Ramai' yang saya maksudkan termasuk pemandu F1 sendiri, tentunya peminat dalam dan luar negara serta pengulas sukan termasuk Brundle yang merupakan bekas pemandu F1. Kesimpulannya mereka merindui Sepang. Dengan GP Bahrain diadakan dengan jayanya dan penuh drama Ahad lalu, their calls are getting louder.

Bagaimanapun seperti yang pernah dikata oleh CEO Sepang International Circuit Azhan Shafriman Hanif, "apabila kita lepaskan Formula 1 ia sangat sukar untuk dapatkan semula". Apa tidaknya. Kalendar tahunan F1 mempunyai had bilangan perlumbaan yang ketat. Apabila Malaysia melepaskan slotnya, banyak negara seluruh dunia masuk queue dan bersaing untuk merebut slot yang ditinggalkan. Oleh itu jika Malaysia serius mahu membawa F1 kembali ke Sepang, negara terpaksa masuk a long waiting list, di samping mengambil kira faktor kos yang amat tinggi dan kos-kos lain yang meningkat. This is stating the obvious, tak perlulah dihuraikan.

Oleh kerana F1 dan Sepang sedang rancak diperkatakan ramai, mari imbau kembali persoalan Malaysia lepaskan F1 in the first place. Kata Najib Razak, waktu itu memegang jawatan perdana menteri, kerajaan beliau terpaksa menamatkan kontrak penganjuran mulai 2018 berikutan pulangan menurun kepada negara berbanding 1999.

"Kerajaan terpaksa tanggung kos penganjuran yang sangat tinggi setiap tahun tetapi pulangan semakin berkurangan termasuk dari segi penonton dan jumlah pelancong asing," kata Najib dipetik media waktu itu. Rasanya ramai masih ingat kata-kata itu. Dalam bahasa mudah: berniaga tak untung.

Tentunya ramai juga yang ingat (kalau lupa sila buat carian Google) Khairy Jamaluddin, ketika itu menteri belia dan sukan, antara individu terawal yang mencadangkan agar Malaysia menghentikan penganjuran F1. Carian Google memaparkan bahawa pada Oktober 2016 Khairy mengeluarkan kenyataan terbuka di Twitter (sekarang X) yang menyarankan kontrak penganjuran di Litar Antarabangsa Sepang ditamatkan. Antara alasan dan hujahnya: Kos terlalu tinggi, pulangan terhad (cited by Najib also), kejatuhan jualan tiket dan penonton televisyen (sedikit sebanyak senada dengan Najib) dan kehilangan kelebihan eksklusif atau novelty.

Sebaliknya Khairy berkata fokus kewangan dan sokongan kepada perlumbaan MotoGP "yang terbukti jauh lebih popular, sentiasa dipenuhi penonton tempatan serta menyaksikan penglibatan pelumba muda Malaysia".

Saya setuju dengan pandangan itu kecuali MotoGP jauh lebih popular daripada F1. Ini tidak tepat. Dua-dua perlumbaan ada peminat tersendiri lantas dua-dua popular. Soal A lebih popular daripada B tidak timbul. Apa pun, alasan kos tinggi yang diberi Najib dan Khairy semasa menamatkan kontrak penganjuran F1 dulu saya akui. Memang kos tinggi dan boleh terus meningkat sekali gus memberi kesan kepada pentadbiran Najib.

Yang saya tidak faham mengapa (menurut Najib dan Khairy) jumlah penonton dan pelancong asing tidak seramai yang diharapkan lantas drop in ticket sales dan penonton televisyen. Pelik kerana setiap perlumbaan F1 di semua litar ia diadakan menyaksikan ia sentiasa mendpat sambutan penonton yang datang ke litar atau menonton perlumbaan di televisyen. Semua negara yang menganjurkan perlumbaan F1 tidak kehilangan pelancong.

Mengapa Malaysia tidak didatangi ramai pelancong lalu penjualan tiket merosot? Apakah kita tidak semeriah negara lain yang menganjurkan perlumbaan F1? Adakah mungkin Malaysia sendiri tidak kuat membuat promosi untuk Sepang?

Aspek novelty yang diketengahkan Khairy agak pelik. Menurut beliau Sepang hilang sinar dengan adanya litar di negara lain seperti Singapura, China, Bahrain dan Abu Dhabi. Khairy mengakui GP Singapura lebih bijak menarik pelancong dengan konsep perlumbaan malam di tengah kota (street race) yang disertakan dengan konsert antarabangsa. Sebaliknya Sepang kekal perlumbaan siang di bawah matahari terik dan kedudukan litar yang jauh dari bandar raya, katanya.
Ya memang Singapura bijak tetapi apa respon kita? Tutup kedai -- hentikan perlumbaan F1 di Sepang. Perlu dinyatakan street races have their share of detractors. Saya tak cadang perincikan.

Mengenai perlumbaan di Sepang diadakan dalam cuaca panas, saya pernah baca laporan yang memetik beberapa pelumba terkemuka menyifatkan Sepang sebagai the hottest circuit in the F1 series. Namun elemen panas dicampur dengan bentuk litar membuatkan Sepang cabaran which they look forward to take on. Di Sepang it's a test for both machine and driver.

Litar Sepang masih di lokasi sama -- jauh daripada Kuala Lumpur. Semasa GP Bahrain diadakan tempoh hari, 100,000 penonton datang. Perlumbaan dianjurkan oleh Bahrain tetapi Malaysia mendapat economic spillover yang menguntungkan. Jadi untuk mengatakan kedudukan Sepang menyumbang kepada kurang penonton dan F1 kurang dapat sambutan di Malaysia boleh dipertikaikan.

Bukan tujuan penulisan ini mengungkit kisah lama cuma saya teringat laporan myMetro 1 Julai lalu mengenai pelanjutan kontrak penganjuran MotoGP di Sepang. Malaysia akan terus menjadi tuan rumah MotoGP dari 2027 hingga 2031 di Litar Antarabangsa Sepang. Semasa membuat pengumuman itu, CEO SIC berkata SIC tidak mahu ulangi kesilapan menamatkan kontrak F1 pada 2018.

Saya tutup penulisan ini dengan memetik perenggan akhir artikel Pengerusi Perbadanan Stadium Malaysia Helmy Haja Mydin yang disiar portal Scoop bertajuk 'The Formula for F1's return to Sepang'. Kata beliau: "Sepang has shown it can still host the world. Whether we pay to do so every year is a question for the spreadsheet and it should be answered there first".

5aab7bda8d58cc55: When the United States and China begin agreeing on the vocabulary of their strategic relationship, Asean should pay close attention.
The September summit between President Donald Trump and President Xi Jinping produced two developments of particular importance.

Washington and Beijing agreed to establish a dialogue on what the United States now calls “super intelligence” (SI), accompanied by a bilateral communication channel for serious SI incidents. The next SI summit is in November 2026.
Second, the relationship was framed in official Chinese reporting around a “constructive relationship of strategic stability.” The phrase is important.
It suggests that the two largest powers are attempting to place intense competition within a framework where cooperation remains possible.
This should not be mistaken for a formal alliance or strategic partnership.

But politically, the language points towards treating China as a constructive strategic interlocutor — and potentially a constructive strategic partner where common interests converge — rather than merely an adversary that must be contained.
Asean should understand the significance.

For years, US-China relations have been defined largely through rivalry: tariffs, semiconductors, Taiwan, the South China Sea, military competition and technological restrictions. None of these disagreements has disappeared.
Yet Washington and Beijing are simultaneously discovering that certain technologies may become too consequential to manage exclusively through competition.
Super intelligence is potentially one of them.
President Trump announced at the United Nations that his administration would use “super intelligence” rather than artificial intelligence.
Following his meeting with Xi, Trump said the Chinese leader appeared receptive to the terminology, while Beijing indicated that it respected Washington’s choice of wording.
Terminology matters.
“Superintelligence” conventionally has a much narrower technical meaning: Intelligence exceeding human capabilities across virtually all cognitive domains.
The Trump administration appears to be using “super intelligence” more broadly as a replacement for AI. These meanings should not be confused.
Nevertheless, the creation of a US-China dialogue on super intelligence is strategically serious.
The two powers are beginning to discuss the risks and benefits associated with advanced AI while creating a channel through which serious incidents can potentially be communicated.
This resembles, conceptually rather than technologically, an embryonic form of crisis management.
During the nuclear age, Washington and Moscow eventually realised that strategic competition required communication precisely because miscalculation could become catastrophic.
AI is not a nuclear weapon. Its development, diffusion and applications are fundamentally different.

Yet the strategic principle is familiar: As technology becomes more powerful, misunderstanding between the powers controlling much of it becomes increasingly dangerous. Asean must therefore be warned.
If Washington and Beijing become the principal architects of the rules surrounding super intelligence, Southeast Asia risks becoming a rule-taker rather than a rule-shaper.
Asean represents almost 700 million people and is rapidly attracting data centres, semiconductor investments, cloud infrastructure and AI-related industries.
Yet much of the frontier technology, computing capacity and foundational architecture remains controlled outside Southeast Asia.
Technological dependence can eventually become strategic dependence.
Asean therefore needs its own position on super intelligence.
This does not mean attempting to compete directly with the United States or China.
Such an ambition would be unrealistic. Malaysia's strength, in particular, has always rested on what can be called Quiescent Diplomacy.
It uses a silent but strategic approach to create sufficient diplomatic and institutional space so that larger powers recognise the importance of Southeast Asia including AI and SI.
Asean, invariably , Malaysia, should insist on meaningful human control over autonomous systems.
This involves stronger cyber security standards. Just as importantly sovereign protection of data. Due safeguards are required to protect critical infrastructure.
As and when regional protocols for dealing with major AI incidents are made more resilient, the region can handle the dawn of the age of SI.
Asean should also use Asean Plus Three, the East Asia Summit and other Asean-led mechanisms to ensure that conversations about advanced AI do not become an exclusively US-China enterprise.
The emerging US-China rapprochement over terminology and strategic stability is encouraging. But it also contains a warning.
Washington and Beijing remain strategic competitors.
Yet they are demonstrating that, where systemic dangers demand it, competition can coexist with constructive strategic cooperation.
Asean must ensure that it has a seat at the table when the rules governing those dangers are written.
The age of artificial intelligence has arrived. If the age of super intelligence follows, Asean cannot afford to wake up after Washington and Beijing have already determined its rules.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
1ab22332aa9b2687: Jet-powered Russian drones recently hit a train in Ukraine a mere mile from the Polish border. The drone pilots, and their Kremlin minders, must have known that officials from Europe, the UK, the US, and elsewhere had previously left Kyiv by train after participating in the Yalta European Strategy (YES) Annual Meeting, a sort of Ukrainian Davos.

But the trains carrying former UK prime minister Boris Johnson, former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt, former CIA director David Petraeus, and former Polish president Aleksander Kwaśniewski, among others, were not hit. Had the Russians missed them intentionally or through incompetence?
Whatever the answer, there is no doubt that Western officials’ continued support for Ukraine, on display at the YES Annual Meeting, rankles the Kremlin.

At the end of one panel, Polish foreign minister Radosław Sikorski candidly remarked that, if attacked, Nato could defeat Russia quite quickly: “If the Ukrainians have knocked out half of Russia’s refining capacity in six months, we could do it in six weeks and take out the other half.” Sikorski later confirmed that he was referring to Nato’s European members.
The Kremlin was stunned by this matter-of-fact remark and quickly went on the offensive, with Russian foreign ministry spokesperson Maria Zakharova calling it “Russophobia”.

Perhaps Kremlin officials have grown accustomed to friendly exchanges with US president Donald Trump’s so-called “negotiators,” Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner—blind amateurs “unburdened with geopolitical detail,” as Edward Luce put it in the Financial Times.
Viktor Sobolev, a member of the State Duma Defense Committee, dismissed the premise: “We don’t plan to attack anyone; the president has said this many times.”

Never mind that Russian president Vladimir Putin also vehemently denied that he had any intention of invading Ukraine and, before that, Georgia. To make his point more clearly about how inoffensive Russia was, Sobolev went on to warn Poles against picking a fight with “a country that possesses nuclear weapons”.

The most pathetic comment came from Putin’s aide Nikolai Patrushev, who accused Sikorski of “Russophobic frenzy” and claimed that Russia poses no threat to anyone because it has no reason to conduct military operations against Europe.

But if Russia were to attack Poland, he added, the country would cease to exist within 2–3 days. (In a subsequent TV interview, Sikorski dismissed Patrushev’s threat, remarking that “2–3 days” is how long it was supposed to take Russia to occupy Kyiv back in 2022.)

The Kremlin is determined to isolate Ukraine. That means not only breaking the will of the country’s backers, but also cutting it off physically by striking merchant ships on the Black Sea and shelling Odesa’s three main ports.

This has paralysed the export of grain at the peak of an exceptional harvest and prevented even the cautious movement of cargo along the coast of Romania and Bulgaria, which will have consequences for Ukraine’s economic survival and world food prices.
Making matters worse, the Danube is so shallow this year that its river ports are practically unusable. And those vessels small enough to enter it risk coming under fire.
A civilian cargo boat en route to Galați, Romania, was recently hit by a Russian drone at the mouth of the Danube, killing the captain and several crew members.

Overland routes are also being disrupted by Russian attacks on Ukrainian border posts. The Starokozache crossing, which leads into Moldova, was recently hit; so was the Mayaki bridge on the same route.
The closures of border checkpoints, no matter how brief, can turn waiting trains and cars into sitting ducks for even the most inexperienced drone operators.

Roads may be slightly less dangerous than rail tracks because itineraries can be changed on short notice. Petraeus, one of the officials almost struck by a Russian drone when leaving Kyiv by train, suggested that next time he might take a car.

These assaults cannot go unanswered, because they isolate Ukraine and embolden Putin to continue testing the West. After this recent train bombing, Nato secretary-general Mark Rutte was asked about the possibility of a Russian attack that could demand the alliance’s response.
He cautioned: “If you are willing to sacrifice 1.2 million of your own people in this crazy unprovoked fight, let’s not be naive about what Putin could do.”

With winter approaching, Ukraine desperately needs help: generators, heaters, warm clothes, and power stations. When the border is shut, bringing aid feels a bit like delivering items for inmates at the prison gates.

But that is precisely what Putin is trying to achieve. He is seeking to destroy an entire country by severing its ties with the outside world. Ukrainians know what awaits them if Putin succeeds. Are the rest of us aware of what we are enabling by failing to act? In Rutte’s words, let’s not be naive.
Anna Husarska, a former senior policy adviser at the International Rescue Committee, is a journalist and political analyst.

21c23ab08aafeb08: As artificial intelligence transforms industries and national security, understanding the latest hardware capabilities is important for maintainind technological advantage. AI accelerators — specialized systems designed to speed up capabilities such as neural networks, deep learning, and machine learning — have been a major area of development for nearly a decade. Since 2018, team from the Lincoln Laboratory Supercomputing Center (LLSC) has been conducting the Lincoln AI Computing Survey (LAICS, pronounced "lace"). Six papers later, LAICS continues to summarize current commercial AI accelerators and compare their peak performance and peak power. "About eight years ago, we saw a sharp rise in the number of research AI accelerators described in research papers and commercial accelerators being announced, and we started to get questions about them from government sponsors of the laboratory's work. That was motivation enough to start the survey," says Albert Reuther, a staff member at the LLSC, which operates and optimizes the high-performance computing systems used by thousands of laboratory research staff. Although AI accelerators are frequently used for processes such as machine learning, they also can enable other parallel applications, such as modeling the functions of molecules and speeding up simulations of fluid dynamics — processes that are very computationally expensive. AI accelerator technology can come in a number of forms: central processing units (CPUs), graphics processing units (GPUs), application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs), and dataflow accelerators. Each type of accelerator has slightly different capabilities. CPUs can be used for general-purpose computing, while ASICs can perform only very specific tasks. Dataflow accelerators, FPGAs, and GPUs are more flexible and can be configured for a variety of workloads. Efficiency and performance vary across the different types of accelerators depending on how they are designed. The goal of LAICS is to survey the technologies currently on the market and compare them to find the best accelerators for certain needs. Led by Reuther, the LAICS team includes LLSC members Michael Jones, Peter Michaleas, Jeremy Kepner, and Vijay Gadepally. The team also collaborates with researchers across Lincoln Laboratory, including in the Advanced Technology Division and Intelligence, Surveillance, and Reconnaissance and Tactical Systems Division, to learn how accelerators support research and development for their missions. The first paper in their series studied 57 accelerators, while the latest one looked at more than 120 accelerators. The main metrics the team uses to compare accelerators are the peak performance and power; then they sort accelerators by whether they're on a chip, card, or system. All the data in the papers are drawn from public sources, which can be challenging because some companies prefer to keep their performance and power data private. To keep up to date on the latest in the field, Reuther runs daily news and citation searches that report new technical press articles, company announcements, and industry presentations. "It continues to surprise me how each year another five to 10 startups get funded and announced, and then release new AI accelerators," Reuther says. "One might think that the landscape is saturated enough, but then another batch of innovative accelerators is introduced." In addition to summarizing the performance versus peak power of the current accelerators, each paper explores a new aspect of the field. For example, the paper published in 2022 investigated sources of performance increases, finding that they stem from smaller, denser transistor designs and the use of lower numerical precision (i.e., calculating fewer significant digits). The latest paper examined different architectural choices available, analyzing how the addition of certain components, such as more cores per processor or parallel performance, would change the system. Reuther plans to continue the survey for the foreseeable future, stating that, in just the past few months, six new startups have announced their first AI accelerators. "AI and the hardware it runs on are such hot topics, and it is important for Lincoln Laboratory to be an unbiased technical advisor for choosing and pursuing the right technologies," Reuther says. "Our AI accelerator surveys have helped many sponsors and government colleagues gain a better understanding of the AI accelerator landscape and make better research and acquisition decisions about them. This survey has also been very valuable to determine which GPUs we should consider for upcoming LLSC system purchases so it not only benefits our sponsors and mission programs, but also benefits all LLSC users." The full set of papers and the accompanying datasets can be found here.
ecc07393279513fe: OpenAI will begin automatically watermarking text generated with ChatGPT in the European Union, the company has announced. It will also offer the watermarking feature in other regions, but it will be off by default outside of the EU.

The move in Europe is driven by a need to comply with the EU AI Act, which took effect in August. It requires marking content produced by AI models in a way that another tool can detect. Unfortunately, there is still no completely effective and reliable way to do that. A few standards already exist, like SynthID and the C2PA project, but they are relatively easy to circumvent for anyone with basic know-how.

The same is likely true for OpenAI's watermark. Its method is proprietary; the company calls it textGrain, and has published a technical paper explaining how it works. But in general, it works like other LLM watermarking tools we've seen in the past: It puts patterns in the word choices that are not clear to a human reader and that don't meaningfully change the general quality of the output, but that someone with a key can use a specialized detector to find. OpenAI says it will be giving access to the detector to a limited number of researchers and organizations and providing a request-for-approval process for others to be added over time.

e81043418dfeb9c4: MIT is launching a new strategic initiative today: MIT for America, which seeks to strengthen STEM education nationally, at many levels of learning.  Addressing a critical national need, the initiative ranges across STEM fields and will engage students from kindergarten through community college, preparing them to live and work in a world increasingly shaped by science and technology. MIT for America’s programs will develop new opportunities for student achievement in mathematics, hands-on design and fabrication, and constructive engagement with artificial intelligence.  President Sally Kornbluth made the announcement today in a letter to the Institute community. “A natural extension of the Institute’s long record of national service, MIT for America is grounded in our deep belief in potential over pedigree, of the transformative power of learning by doing and in the open sharing of knowledge,” Kornbluth wrote. The initiative represents an Institute-wide effort to address the national challenge of improving STEM education and helping it adapt to shifting societal needs. MIT for America will leverage the Institute’s longstanding strengths to develop new programs and expand existing projects, while amplifying MIT’s impact on national education. MIT for America’s faculty leaders emphasize that the initiative will support programs that can be scaled up and that provide direct, face-to-face guidance for learners and educators.  “The goal is to provide programs that are both scalable and high-touch, and make an impact across the country,” says Professor Eric Klopfer, a faculty co-director of MIT for America and director of the Scheller Teacher Education Program and the Education Arcade at MIT. “All our programs take advantage of things we are well-positioned to do at MIT, and can be distributed around the country. That’s our guiding light.”  Cynthia Breazeal, faculty co-director of MIT for America, professor of media arts and sciences, and the Benesse Professor of Research in Education, says the initiative “is about bringing high-quality access to STEM and AI education, from kindergarten to community college, across the United States. We live in an innovation-driven world, and it’s important to have an education that gives you access to it, whether that’s so you can be a fully engaged citizen or have the opportunity for economic mobility.” Breazeal adds: “Talent is everywhere. We think opportunity should be, too.”  The initiative is addressing large-scale needs in STEM education. Only 29 percent of U.S. students in grades 9-12 build circuits, and only 6 percent of students enroll in computer science classes, even though about 60 percent of high schools offer such courses. MIT for America intends to substantially help communities across the country build the bandwidth needed to further develop STEM knowledge and workplace skills.  “This effort is about really rolling up sleeves and getting out there and engaging communities, and helping to build capacity across the United States,” Breazeal adds. MIT for America features programs addressing three high-priority areas: Mathematical thinking and problem solving: Work here builds on an existing program, the MIT for America Calculus Project, launched a year ago, in which MIT students and alumni volunteer to help provide calculus tutoring to students in school districts across the country.  Living, learning, and working with AI: This area addresses multiple issues revolving around AI, including teacher education that helps instructors integrate AI into classroom learning in productive ways, and programs that enhance AI skills and STEM education in technical-vocational schools and community colleges. The MIT RAISE program (Responsible AI for Social Empowerment and Education) is a leader in this domain.  Designing, making, and innovating: MIT for America plans to build out programs that encourage hands-on learning, design work, use of fab labs and makerspaces, and experiential learning, sometimes deploying tools such as national design challenges.  “Across the U.S., we want to unlock opportunities and experiences where students are,” says Claudia Urrea, head of MIT for America and head of the MIT pK-12 Initiative. “We want to find people who have not had the opportunity to discover their talent.” In the first case, the MIT for America Calculus Project provides a ready model of outreach with growth potential. About half of U.S. school districts offer calculus, but many of those districts may be under-resourced. The MIT for America Calculus Project has been growing in partnership with an increasing number of school districts, while MIT undergraduates and alumni have enjoyed participating in the program.   “People have been really excited about the MIT for America Calculus Project, seeing both the impact that it has, and its model, which I think has resonated,” Klopfer says. “That’s really representative of what other programs could look like.” In the second topic area, MIT for America can leverage burgeoning efforts such as MIT RAISE. The program helps educate teachers and engage students about implementing AI in ways that can complement the developing skills of students, enabling them to use AI in productive ways. “RAISE is about providing materials and training for teachers that helps them have conversations and productive activities around AI,” Klopfer says. “It’s about understanding how AI works and discussing what the values are in your school. It has to be active, involving the students. If you try to force things, about AI one way or the other, that will fail.” In an outgrowth of RAISE, MIT also launched a related program, Pathways for AI Training and Hiring (PATH), on Oct. 1. Starting with a partnership with Georgia State University, PATH aims to bring AI training to two-year and four-year colleges, to help students gain AI skills useful for workplaces.  “RAISE has had a lot of success with scaling already,” Breazeal says, noting that about 1 million students were involved with RAISE’s Day of AI event earlier this year. “At MIT, we want to empower youth voices to shape the future. It’s an excellent example of our ability to do that.” And in the third topic area, MIT for America can help produce substantial growth in programs aimed at hands-on learning. That may include more projects such as MIT’s Regenerative Futures Challenge, a global program stemming from MIT’s pK-12 Initiative, which give students the opportunity to create climate and sustainability solutions. Additionally, the Fab Foundation, which grew out of MIT’s Center for Bits and Atoms Fab Lab program, offers tools and curriculum to learners at 300 fab labs across the U.S. “It’s about coming together in places where there are people who can work together, mentor each other, and learn by example,” Klopfer says. “That’s the kind of thing we want to be creating at scale. We want to build on that.” All told, MIT for America represents a vigorous all-campus effort to enhance education through sustained outreach and knowledge-sharing. At MIT, partners in creating the initiative include the MIT Media Lab; MIT RAISE; the MIT pK-12 Initiative; the Office of the Vice President for Resource Development; and the Office of Innovation and Strategy. The leaders of MIT for America presented an overview of the program in September at MIT’s Alumni Leadership Conference, and they say alumni activity around the new initiative will be another key to its success.  “We really appreciate the support and engagement of our alumni,” Breazeal says. “We know they care about K-12 education and access to community colleges.” More broadly, she adds, “We do think this message will resonate with people all across the country.” “I look forward to watching these programs flourish, evolve, and grow,” Kornbluth wrote to the community.

f1decbf03cfffea5: The publisher of Wikipedia said Monday that OpenAI agents attempted to hack a note-taking tool it hosts, made unauthorized edits, and sent millions of resource-intensive requests to its infrastructure, in the latest instance of OpenAI systems taking harmful and potentially dangerous actions.

The objective of some of the OpenAI agents’ actions, the Wikimedia Foundation said, was to use Wikipedia as a proxy for fetching data from third-party sites. In one case, the agents posted “malicious edits” that were intended to repurpose a citation tool as a proxy. In another, the agents made unsuccessful attempts to compromise the Wikipedia Etherpad note-taking tool so it would serve the same purpose.

029f0b40edc8d12d: From Salahuddin Hamzah
I refer to a column by Tajuddin Rasdi, published on Oct 5.

I am furious with this theory. The writer’s argument, which suggests that Malays accept corruption, has little merit and is substantially unfair because it omits many important historical events. Let’s look back at the timeline.

Between 2014 and 2018, corruption was perceived to be at its peak due to the 1MDB scandal. What happened afterwards? Umno-Barisan Nasional was overwhelmingly voted out by the rakyat after ruling the country for 60 years.
In 2022, BN only won 30 seats. Isn’t it evident that the perceived corruption was rejected by the Malays?

After each defeat, Umno accepted the result wholeheartedly and openly welcomed investigations into allegations of corruption. Many leaders paid a heavy price, either through jail time, fines, or damage to their reputations. The leadership repeatedly called for the party's revival. Yet the writer has refused to factor this into his argument.
The writer also claims that the majority of Malays pay little to no tax. This is an old song.

In reality, a large segment of Malaysia’s M40 population are Malays, and they pay taxes. The M40 are also largely working-class salaried employees, meaning the taxes they owe are automatically deducted from their income, leaving little room for tax avoidance.
In comparison, many of the much wealthier T20 taxpayers are business owners, where tax costs can potentially be transferred to consumers.
Let’s not even go into the largely non-Malay-dominated black market, which operates tax-free and involves billions of ringgit.

Regarding DAP as the bogeyman, the writer seems unable to accept the very nature of democracy – voters can choose freely. DAP being dominated by one race simply does not appeal to the majority of Malays. Marketing wise, DAP is a failure. But the writer refuses to acknowledge this.
The Malays' lack of preference for DAP is instead portrayed as an acceptance of corruption. What kind of argument is this?
I firmly believe that the conscience of the Malays is entirely clear – Malays do not accept corruption. Any argument suggesting otherwise is simply racist and simplistic.
When former prime minister Najib Razak was convicted, Umno accepted the judgment with an open heart and "keinsafan" (remorse).
No one took to the streets claiming that the conviction was illegitimate. Umno only sought a royal pardon, which is a form of clemency provided for under the Federal Constitution.

The leniency shown by some Malays towards Najib is in no way an acceptance of corruption. It is substantially fuelled by the frustration that after Umno’s defeat, things do not seem to have gotten better.
Najib deserves his partial pardon considering his significant contributions to the country, despite the shortcomings.
I reject the writer’s theory.
Salahuddin Hamzah is an Umno Youth member and an FMT reader.

a4beae4315c8e89c: From Syerleena Abdul Rashid
I keep thinking about the plans Irene Sofiya Khairool Faisal had made with her friends.

After their examinations, they wanted to spend some time together, celebrate their birthdays, dress up and go out for coffee. They were ordinary teenage plans. The kind young people make without imagining that anything could stop them. Irene was 16. She wanted to become a doctor, like her late mother. On Oct 3, she was found badly injured inside her school hall in Yong Peng. She died before help arrived.

A student has been remanded and the police are investigating the case as murder. The motive has not been established, so we should not speculate or try the case on social media. Still, one fact should trouble every parent in this country – Irene went to school and never came home.

Just days later, Parliament was told that 5,681 bullying cases had been reported in schools between January and August this year. The cases included physical, verbal, non-verbal and cyberbullying. Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim himself acknowledged that the real number could be higher because some cases might have gone unreported.
That number bothers me. But what bothers me even more are the children who may not be included in it.

How many kept quiet because they were frightened? How many tried to tell an adult but were dismissed? How many parents were told that it was only a misunderstanding between students? How many schools worry more about their reputation than the child asking for help?
We have been here before.

Last year, Malaysians were shaken by the death of 13-year-old Zara Qairina Mahathir, who was found unconscious near her boarding-school dormitory in Sabah. An inquest into the circumstances of her death has been ongoing, alongside separate proceedings involving allegations of bullying. We must allow those legal processes to establish the truth. Zara deserves facts, not rumours.

We also remember Zulfarhan Osman Zulkarnain, who was tortured by fellow university students and died from his injuries in 2017. Seven years later, the Court of Appeal convicted six former students of his murder.

These cases are different. We should not pretend that every school incident has the same cause or circumstances. But each of them forces us to ask whether the adults, rules and institutions surrounding our children are doing enough to keep them safe.
The honest answer is that we are still falling short.

I appreciate the prime minister’s willingness to admit that current measures are not enough. The government has increased counselling support, trained wardens, strengthened disciplinary procedures and mental-health screening, and allowed the police greater access to schools. More CCTV cameras are also planned.

These steps matter. But installing cameras cannot be the whole answer. A camera may record what happened. It cannot comfort a frightened child, notice a sudden change in behaviour or ask why a student has stopped eating, talking or attending class.
That requires people who are trained, alert and prepared to act.

Every serious complaint should have a clear deadline for action. The child must first be placed somewhere safe. Evidence must be preserved. Parents must be informed. Counselling and medical support must be available immediately. If a possible crime is involved, the police and child-protection authorities must be notified.

Children also need a way to report abuse outside the immediate school hierarchy. It is extremely difficult for a young person to complain when the alleged bully is a senior student, or when the person who ignored the earlier complaint is someone in authority.

We should also publish anonymised data regularly. How many complaints were received? How many were investigated? How long did schools take to respond? How many were referred to the police? What support was provided to the victims?

This is not about humiliating teachers or treating every school as unsafe. Most teachers work extremely hard and care deeply about their students. It is about ensuring that those who do their jobs properly are supported, while those who conceal complaints or fail to protect children are held accountable.

Parents have responsibilities as well. We must pay attention when our children become unusually quiet, angry or afraid to attend school. We must listen before blaming them or telling them to toughen up. But parents cannot be inside classrooms, corridors and hostels throughout the day. Once a child enters the school gate, the institution assumes a duty of care. That responsibility cannot disappear when something goes wrong.
Bullying is not character-building. Fear is not discipline. Keeping quiet does not protect a school’s good name.

A school earns its reputation when children feel safe enough to learn, speak and ask for help. That is the standard we should insist upon, because no family should have to send a child to school in the morning and spend the evening wondering why that child never came home.
Syerleena Abdul Rashid is the Bukit Bendera MP.
